### Summary The MSP RLE decoder expands run-length data into an in-memory buffer with no cap tied to the declared image size. A small file that passes the pixel-count check can force hundreds of megabytes or more of allocation when the application loads pixels.  ### Details The MSP decoder writes each run into an unbounded `io.BytesIO` and can expand roughly 85x per run:  - `src/PIL/MspImagePlugin.py:144-146`  ### Impact Memory-exhaustion denial of service from a tiny crafted image in any application that loads pixels. The expansion is decoupled from the declared pixel count, so `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` does not bound it.

``` ============================================================================ Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:94  in _tiffWriteProc() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  Pillow can write attacker-chosen data past the end of a heap buffer when it saves a TIFF image to an in-memory destination such as `io.BytesIO` rather than to a file. The same code also copies leftover heap memory from the process into the saved file. Anyone who can supply an image to a service that opens it and re-saves it as TIFF this way can trigger this with default settings. The attached reproducer crashes the process, and the overflow could potentially be developed further, but code execution is not demonstrated here.  The bug is in `_tiffWriteProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. This is the write callback for the in-memory sink that Pillow gives libtiff whenever the save target has no `fileno()`. While writing the directory, libtiff seeks past the current end of data and writes tag values there. `_tiffWriteProc` sizes its `realloc()` from `state->size + size` instead of from the write position `state->loc`. As a result, the first out-of-line tag value written after that seek can run past the allocation by up to the size of the directory: 12 bytes per entry, 126 bytes in the minimal case, and 2384 bytes observed with a 331-entry directory. The overflowing bytes are the tail of a tag value taken from the uploaded file.  No save options are needed, because compression and tags are inherited from the source image. The overflow does require an attacker-sized out-of-line tag to reach libtiff. That happens when the opened TIFF is saved directly (ImageDescription, DocumentName or XMP), or through an embedded ICC profile, which survives `copy()` in `im.info`. The bytes libtiff skips for alignment are never initialised, so any compressed TIFF over 64 KiB written this way also leaks one stale heap byte per padding hole. That leak needs no crafted tag.  The attached reproducer builds a 131 KB PackBits TIFF and runs `Image.open(...).save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF")`. Saving the same image to a file path succeeds, but the `BytesIO` save aborts with glibc's `malloc(): corrupted top size`. A second part of the script shows uninitialised heap bytes at the padding offsets of a `BytesIO` save that are zero in the file save. Saves to real files are unaffected. The defect dates to e782fe721e01 (2013) and has been present since Pillow 2.0.0.  ## Details  When `im.save()` writes a TIFF through libtiff to a target that has no usable `fileno()` (`io.BytesIO`, an HTTP response object, a storage backend stream), libtiff is opened with `TIFFClientOpen()` on Pillow's own in-memory sink, `_tiffWriteProc` / `_tiffSeekProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. libtiff treats that sink like a file: when it writes the directory it seeks *beyond* the current end of data (to `eof + IFD size`, where the out-of-line tag values go, and one byte further after every odd-length tag value to keep offsets even) and writes there. On a real file the kernel grows the file and zero-fills the gap. The memory sink does neither correctly:  1. `_tiffWriteProc` sizes its `realloc()` from `state->size + size` instead of `state->loc + size`, so the first write after such a seek can land past the end of the new allocation — a heap buffer overflow whose content is tag data taken from the image being saved. 2. The bytes that libtiff skips are never written, and the grown region is a bare `realloc()`, so they reach the output TIFF with whatever the heap held before.  Both are reachable with default settings by the ordinary "re-encode the upload" sequence `Image.open(upload); im.save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF")` with no save options: `compression` defaults to the source file's (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1734`), any compression other than raw selects the libtiff writer (`:1746`), the source's `tag_v2` entries are passed through to libtiff (`:1959`), and a target without `fileno()` leaves `_fp = 0` (`:1928-1935`), i.e. the memory sink. The overflow half additionally needs an attacker-controlled out-of-line tag value of the right length to reach libtiff. With the opened `TiffImageFile` saved directly (`tag_v2` passthrough) that can be a ~64 KiB ASCII tag (269/270/271/272) or the XMP packet (tag 700, type BYTE — arbitrary bytes), and the number of tags the upload carries sets the IFD size, i.e. the overrun length (12 bytes per entry; 2384 bytes with a 331-entry IFD observed). After `convert()`/`resize()`/`thumbnail()`/`copy()` the `tag_v2` entries are gone, but `im.info["compression"]` (still selecting libtiff) and `im.info["icc_profile"]` survive and the ICC profile is written as tag 34675 (`:1822-1824`), an equally attacker-controlled out-of-line value: `Image.open(x).copy().save(BytesIO(), "TIFF")` with the payload in the ICC profile produces the identical ASan report. The stale-byte half needs no attacker tag at all.  **Proof (overflow).** A 131 198-byte hand-built TIFF — mode L, 7×8191, `Compression=32773` (PackBits), an `ImageDescription` of 65 535 characters — opened with `Image.open()` and saved with `im.save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF")` aborts a stock build with glibc's `malloc(): corrupted top size`. The same call against an AddressSanitizer build of the C extensions reports  ``` AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow ... WRITE of size 65536  #1 _tiffWriteProc src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:115  #4 TIFFFlush  #5 ImagingLibTiffEncode src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1056 0 bytes to the right of 131072-byte region, allocated by realloc in _tiffWriteProc src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:103 ```  **Proof (uninitialised bytes).** Saving one 300×300 RGB image as `compression="tiff_lzw"` with four odd-length ASCII tags to a `BytesIO`, once with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=1` (glibc fills fresh allocations with 0xfe) and once with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170` (0x55), gives two 369 463-byte TIFFs that differ in exactly 4 bytes, 0xfe vs 0x55, at offsets 369177, 369417, 369423, 369451 — the pad byte between the odd-length last strip and the IFD, and the pad byte after each odd-length tag value except the last. The same save to a filename gives byte-identical files with 0x00 there. Without any allocator tweaks, after a few 64 KB–400 KB Python `bytes` objects filled with 0xa7 are created and freed, re-saving an uploaded LZW TIFF carrying ten odd-length ASCII tags yields 0xa7 at all nine pad offsets.  ### Code walk-through  The sink's state is `{data, size (allocated), loc (position), eof (high-water mark)}`; the encoder path starts it as a zeroed 64 KiB block (`TiffDecode.c:863`, `calloc(bufsize, 1)` with `bufsize = 64*1024`, `flrealloc = 1`). Seeking is unconstrained:  ```c /* src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:124-141  _tiffSeekProc */     case 0: state->loc = off;            break;   /* may exceed eof and size */     case 1: state->loc += off;           break;     case 2: state->loc = state->eof + off; break; ```  and writing assumes `loc <= size`:  ```c /* src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:90-117  _tiffWriteProc */     to_write = MIN(size, state->size - (tsize_t)state->loc);   /* negative if loc > size */     if (state->flrealloc && size > to_write) {         tsize_t newsize = state->size;         while (newsize < (size + state->size)) {               /* capacity target ignores loc */             …             newsize += 64 * 1024;         }         new_data = realloc(state->data, newsize);              /* tail left uninitialised */         …         state->size = newsize;         to_write = size;     }     _TIFFmemcpy((UINT8 *)state->data + state->loc, buf, to_write);   /* :115 */     state->loc += (toff_t)to_write;     state->eof = MAX(state->loc, state->eof); ```  A gdb trace of the sink calls during the overflowing save (stock build, breakpoints on the two procs) shows how libtiff drives it:  ``` write size=63064 at loc=8      (eof=8     size=65536)     strip data (PackBits re-encode: write size=2464  at loc=63072  (eof=63072 size=65536)      8 bytes/row × 8191 rows) seek  off=0     whence=2       -> loc=65536 = eof = size   TIFFWriteDirectory: end of data, already even seek  off=4;  write size=4 at loc=4                        link IFD offset into header seek  off=65662 whence=0       (eof=65536 size=65536)      65536 + 126-byte IFD (10 entries) = tag data area write size=65536 at loc=65662  (eof=65536 size=65536)      ImageDescription, first out-of-line value ```  For that last call `to_write = 65536 − 65662 = −126`, the loop grows `newsize` until it is ≥ `65536 + 65536`, i.e. to 131072, and the `memcpy` writes `[65662, 131198)` into a 131072-byte block: 126 bytes past the end, containing the last 126 bytes of the description string. `loc`/`eof` become 131198 > `size`; `ImagingLibTiffEncode` later sets `size = eof` (`:1067`) and copies `[0, eof)` out of the same block (`:1073`), reading past it as well.  The general condition is: at directory-write time the strip data ends within *IFD-size* bytes of the current allocation boundary, and the first out-of-line tag value has a length just below a multiple of 64 KiB. The overrun length is `IFD size + pad − slack`, so it grows by 12 bytes per additional tag. For single-band images (L, P, 1, I;16, F…) `BitsPerSample` is stored inline and the first out-of-line value in tag order is `DocumentName` (269) or `ImageDescription` (270) — both free-length ASCII strings taken from the source file. Pillow re-encodes the pixels itself, but with PackBits the compressed size is a deterministic function of attacker-chosen pixel rows (the reproducer uses rows of 7 distinct bytes → 8 bytes per row → exactly 65536 bytes including the 8-byte header), so the attacker controls both quantities. For multi-band images the 6-byte `BitsPerSample` array is written first and absorbs the growth, which is why RGB sources do not hit the overflow.  The disclosure half is the benign version of the same sequence. In the LZW/RGB trace the strip data ends at the odd offset 369177; libtiff places the IFD at 369178 and the tag values from 369364 on, and after each odd-length value seeks one byte forward before the next write (`seek off=369418 (loc=369417)`, `write size=5 at loc=369418`, …). Offsets 369177, 369417, 369423 and 369451 are therefore never written. They lie in the part of the buffer obtained by the `realloc()` calls at `:103` (the block grew 65536 → 196608 → 327680 → 458752 during the strip writes), which is not cleared, so the emitted file carries the previous heap contents at those positions. Holes that fall inside the initial 64 KiB are zero only because that block is `calloc`'d.  The defect was introduced in e782fe721e01 ("initial merge of wiredfool/Python-Imaging-Library-G4-Tiff-Support", 2013-03-08), first released in Pillow 2.0.0.  ## Impact  Any service that accepts an image and produces a TIFF rendition into a non-file object — the usual pattern for returning or uploading the result without touching disk — is exposed to whoever supplies the image, with no non-default Pillow setting involved. The overflow additionally requires that an attacker-controlled out-of-line tag value reaches libtiff: the uploaded ImageDescription/DocumentName/XMP when the application saves the opened TIFF itself (or copies its tags into the save), or the embedded ICC profile, which survives `convert()`/`resize()`/`thumbnail()`/`copy()` in `im.info` together with the compression. Under those conditions, with a crafted single-band TIFF the uploader gets a heap out-of-bounds write in the worker process of IFD-size bytes (12 bytes per directory entry the upload carries — 126 bytes with the minimal reproducer, 2384 bytes with a 331-entry IFD) immediately past a 128 KiB-class `realloc` block, with the overwritten bytes being the tail of a tag value they chose; on the stock build the minimal reproducer is detected by glibc and kills the process (`SIGABRT`).  Given two addresses leaked by a separate bug, this write has been turned into code execution against a stock build of this commit with ASLR/PIE/NX enabled and default settings (that proof-of-concept is not included with this report): a single-process stdlib `http.server` worker doing nothing but `Image.open(BytesIO(body)).save(BytesIO(), "TIFF")` per upload executed an attacker-chosen shell command (`id>/tmp/r.XXXXXX`), answered `200` and kept serving (12/12 against a freshly started worker, 2/6 after twenty unrelated uploads; a miss normally leaves the worker running and is retryable). The two addresses (`&system`, `&PyBytes_Type`) were taken from an unrelated information disclosure in the same process; everything else is this bug plus properties of Pillow's TIFF reader used as a heap-shaping script. The 4.7 MB attack TIFF is a 397×165 8-bit PackBits image whose rows re-encode to exactly 65 528 bytes (strip ends at sink offset 65 536), a 63 942-byte XMP packet (tag 700) as the first out-of-line value, and ~500 private IFD entries. Because `TiffImagePlugin` turns every IFD entry into one `bytes` object in IFD order, frees an earlier entry when a later one repeats its tag number, and parses the IFD three times per request (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1258`, `:1271`, and `getexif()` from `load_end()` at `:1331`), those entries drain glibc's free lists, punch exact-size holes for every large allocation the save makes, and arrange that the 128 KiB `realloc` of the sink lands directly below a live 0x540 chunk followed by libtiff's own `TIFF` handle (`malloc(1313)` from `TIFFClientOpen`). The 2384 overflowing bytes rewrite the start of the `TIFF` struct with the command string, a zeroed `tif_dir`, `tif_diroff = 65536`, and `tif_cleanup = system` at +0x3f8; libtiff resumes `TIFFWriteDirectorySec` on the modified handle and calls `(*tif->tif_cleanup)(tif)`. With gdb on `__libc_system` the call arrives as `__libc_system("id>/tmp/r.…") ← libtiff.so.6 ← TIFFFlush ← ImagingLibTiffEncode (src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1056) ← _encode (src/encode.c:139)`. Offsets are per-binary constants (glibc 2.36, CPython 3.12.14, libtiff 4.5.0, this `_imaging.so`), all obtainable from public distribution files.  Independently, every compressed TIFF written to such a target that exceeds 64 KiB discloses one byte of stale heap per alignment hole (one per odd-length tag value plus possibly one before the IFD; the count is set by the tags in the uploaded file) at predictable offsets in the returned file — low bandwidth, but it is other requests' freed data. File-path and real-fd targets (`TIFFFdOpen`) are unaffected by either issue. The primitive is the same class and attacker position as the `TiffDecode.c` decode-side heap overflows CVE-2020-35654, CVE-2021-25289 and CVE-2020-10379, but on the encode path and behind the output-to-a-non-file and tag-passthrough preconditions above, with code execution additionally depending on an address leak from another bug.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script that uses the installed Pillow, writes its inputs into a temporary directory. It has two parts. Each part compares saving to a file path, which goes through `TIFFFdOpen` and is correct, with the same save into an `io.BytesIO`, which goes through the `_tiffWriteProc` memory sink.  **Part 1: heap overflow.** `setup_env()` builds `upload.tif` (131 198 bytes) byte by byte: a mode L, 7×8191 image with `Compression=32773` (PackBits) and a 65 535-character `ImageDescription`. The sizes are picked so that when Pillow re-encodes the pixels, the strip comes to 8 + 8191 × 8 = 65 536 bytes and ends exactly at the sink's initial 64 KiB buffer. libtiff then seeks past the 126-byte IFD and writes the 65 536-byte description at offset 65 662. The sink grows only to 131 072 bytes, so the last 126 bytes of the description are written past the end of the heap block. In a fresh child process, the script runs `Image.open("upload.tif").save(<target>, "TIFF")` with no options, once with `"out.tif"` as the target and once with `io.BytesIO()`. The file save exits with 0. The BytesIO save is killed by SIGABRT, with glibc reporting `malloc(): corrupted top size`.  **Part 2: stale heap bytes in the output.** A child started with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170` (glibc fills fresh allocations with 0x55) saves a seeded-noise 300×300 RGB image with `compression="tiff_lzw"` and four odd-length ASCII tags. It saves once to a file and once to a BytesIO, then prints every offset where the two outputs differ. libtiff skips one pad byte before the IFD and one after each odd-length tag value. The file has 0x00 at those offsets, but the BytesIO output still holds the 0x55 that was in uninitialised `realloc()` memory.  Expected output on this tree:  ``` upload.tif: 131198 bytes save to file path : exit code 0, out.tif = 131210 bytes save to BytesIO   : exit code -6, stderr: 'malloc(): corrupted top size' -> heap overflow crashed the process: True  same image, same options, saved to a file path vs. to a BytesIO:   offset 369177: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55   offset 369417: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55   offset 369423: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55   offset 369451: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55  -> BytesIO output contains never-written heap bytes: True  BUG ```  The last line is `BUG` if either part shows its defect, and `OK` otherwise. With the attached patch applied and rebuilt, the BytesIO save exits with 0, the two outputs are identical, and the script prints `OK`.  ## Suggested fix  The attached patch makes `_tiffWriteProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` honour sparse-file semantics: it sizes the buffer from the write position, and zeroes what `realloc()` adds (the initial block is already `calloc`'d, so every byte libtiff skips then reads as 0, exactly as through `TIFFFdOpen`). For the non-reallocating case (`flrealloc == 0`), where `loc > size` would also make `to_write` negative, it rejects the write with a `TIFFError`, the same idiom `_tiffReadProc` uses:  ```diff -        while (newsize < (size + state->size)) { +        while (newsize < (size + (tsize_t)state->loc)) {  … +        memset((UINT8 *)new_data + state->size, 0, newsize - state->size);          state->data = new_data;          state->size = newsize;          to_write = size; +    } else if (to_write < 0) { +        TIFFError("_tiffWriteProc", "Invalid Write at loc %" PRIu64 ", size: %" PRIu64, …); +        return 0;      } ```  `_tiffSeekProc` is left unconstrained, since libtiff legitimately seeks past the end of data; with the write proc fixed, `eof` can no longer exceed `size`, so the read-out in `ImagingLibTiffEncode` (`:1067`, `:1073`) stays within the block. The patch also adds `test_save_bytesio_seek_past_end` to `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py`, which saves the PackBits 64 KiB-boundary case and an LZW case with odd-length tags to both a file and a `BytesIO` and asserts the outputs are identical. With the patch applied and rebuilt, the BytesIO output is byte-identical to the file output, no AddressSanitizer report is produced for tag lengths 65410/65535/131071/196607, the code-execution chain described under Impact no longer runs its command, and the existing TIFF tests pass.  ## The patch  Size the libtiff in-memory write buffer from the write position, not its current size, and zero the space added by realloc in _tiffWriteProc  Applies to `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` at the commit above.  ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py index 3d804ea4a..d2a926a62 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py @@ -760,6 +760,38 @@ class TestFileLibTiff(LibTiffTestCase):          save_bytesio("packbits")          save_bytesio("tiff_lzw")   +    def test_save_bytesio_seek_past_end(self, tmp_path: Path) -> None: +        # When writing the directory, libtiff seeks past the end of the data +        # written so far, and then writes the tag values there. ## Summary BmpRleDecoder can be forced to allocate gigabytes of memory from a kilobyte-sized crafted BMP file via unbounded growth in the delta escape and absolute mode branches.  ## Affected versions All versions up to and including current HEAD (v13.0.0.dev0, commit e7a7ea84)  ## Root cause BmpRleDecoder.decode() (BmpImagePlugin.py:327-395) builds a Python bytearray `data` with dest_length = xsize*ysize, looping `while len(data) < dest_length`. The loop condition is only checked at the TOP; individual branches append attacker-controlled amounts UNBOUNDED by dest_length:  - delta escape (line 370): data += b"\x00" * (right + up * self.state.xsize) with right,up in 0..255 -> up to ~255*xsize bytes in ONE iteration. - absolute mode (line 385): data += bytes_read (up to 255).  Because a single delta can push len(data) to ~256 * (row size), a tiny RLE stream combined with a large-but-legal xsize (xsize*ysize just under MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, ~89M) yields a multi-GB `data` bytearray (then copied again by bytes(data) and set_as_raw). No heap OOB (bytearray/set_as_raw are bounds-safe), but a severe memory-amplification DoS: the attacker file stays tiny.  ## Reproduction Python 3.13, Pillow HEAD e7a7ea84  Attached: pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py  A 1084-byte BMP (BI_RLE8, width=3,000,000, height=1 -> 3M px, passes bomb check) with one delta escape (00 02 00 150) produces ~429 MB `data`; measured peak RSS 911 MB. Scaling width toward the bomb limit and up=255 produces tens of GB from a ~1 KB file.  ## Suggested fix Cap growth at dest_length in the delta and absolute branches, e.g. clamp the delta fill to (dest_length - len(data)) and stop appending once len(data) >= dest_length; reject deltas that would move the cursor beyond the image, matching the existing per-row clamp at line 341-343.  Credit: Yazan Balawneh - CyStack Security Team (GitHub: sonicnew)  [pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30244974/pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py)

### Summary Pillow's documented PDF append path can spend disproportionate CPU time on a compact malformed PDF page tree.  An attacker who can supply an existing PDF to an application that appends an image with `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)` can provide a malformed `/Pages` tree where each level repeats the same child `/Pages` reference in `/Kids`. Pillow treats the graph as a tree and expands each repeated reference in `PdfParser.linearize_page_tree()` without tracking visited or duplicate indirect references.  In the bounded proof below, a `1410`-byte PDF expands to `8192` page references from one distinct page object and takes about `9.6` seconds through the append path. A comparable linear control with the same depth stays at one page reference and completes in about `0.02` seconds.  This is in scope for Pillow's security policy because it is reproducible in `main`, affects the latest public release tested (`12.3.0`), and is not just an unexpected Python exception. Applications are impacted if untrusted users can supply an existing PDF that the application later appends to, watermarks, or exports using Pillow's `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)` route. The proof does not demonstrate confidentiality impact, integrity impact, memory corruption, filesystem access, network access, or impact through ordinary `Image.open()`. ``` ============================================================================ Heap buffer overflow writing JPEG comment after ICC profile fills buffer Location: src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:330  in ImagingJpegEncode() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  A heap buffer overflow in Pillow's JPEG encoder lets anyone who can supply an image write up to 64 KB of bytes they choose, followed by the rest of the compressed image, past the end of a 64 KB heap buffer. The target is any application that re-saves the image as JPEG while keeping its colour profile. The reliable result is that the Python process is killed outright rather than raising an exception. Because the overwritten memory sits directly in front of function pointers that the encoder calls next, this could allow code execution, though the attached reproducer demonstrates only the crash.  The bug is in `ImagingJpegEncode()` in `src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`. State 4 (line 330) calls `jpeg_write_marker()` for the COM comment marker without checking that the output buffer has room. Meanwhile, `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes that buffer from the EXIF and ICC/XMP data only and reserves nothing for the comment. When a 65498-byte ICC profile fills the 65536-byte buffer exactly, libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores one byte past the end and then decrements `free_in_buffer` from 0. The `size_t` counter wraps, so the marker, the comment and the entire compressed image are written out of bounds.  Triggering it takes only a valid JPEG (or PNG) carrying that profile and any comment, passed through `Image.open()` and then `im.save(..., "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile"))`. That is the documented way to preserve colour. The comment is forwarded from `im.info` automatically, and no non-default setting is involved.  The attached reproducer re-saves such a file on the stock build, and the process dies with SIGSEGV. An identical file without the comment saves normally. An ASan build of Pillow will not flag this, because the stray writes happen inside the system libjpeg-turbo. Valgrind does report it, as an invalid write immediately after the 65569-byte allocation.  The unguarded call was introduced in e50ae85ea406 ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0.  ## Details  `ImagingJpegEncode()` (`src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`) is a resumable state machine that fills a caller-supplied output buffer of `bytes` bytes and returns when it is full. State 4 writes the JPEG COM marker with `jpeg_write_marker()` without first checking that the buffer has any room left. When the preceding state 3 — the verbatim copy of the "extra" APP segments (ICC profile / XMP) — ends exactly at the last byte of the buffer, `jpeg_write_marker()` is entered with `free_in_buffer == 0`. libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores the byte first and tests `--free_in_buffer == 0` afterwards, so the `size_t` counter wraps to 2^64-1 instead of triggering the "buffer full" path, and the 4-byte marker header, the whole comment, and then (state 5) the DQT/SOF/DHT/SOS headers and the entire entropy-coded image are written linearly past the end of the 65536-byte heap buffer allocated in `src/encode.c`.  A JPEG laid out as  ``` FFD8                                   SOI FFE2 <len> "ICC_PROFILE\0" 01 01 <65498 bytes>     -> im.info["icc_profile"] FFFE <len> <comment, any length 1..65533>           -> im.info["comment"] <any baseline RGB JPEG body> ```  opened with `Image.open()` and re-saved with the usual colour-profile-preserving call  ```python im.save(out, "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")) ```  kills the Python process on the stock build at this commit: glibc aborts with `realloc(): invalid next size` / `corrupted size vs. prev_size`, or the process takes SIGSEGV inside `jpeg_write_marker`/`jpeg_write_scanlines`. Stopping at `JpegEncode.c:330` in gdb shows `next_output_byte - buf == 65536`, `free_in_buffer == 0`, `comment_size == 65533` before the call, and `next_output_byte - buf == 131073`, `free_in_buffer == 18446744073709486079` after it — 65537 bytes already written beyond a 65536-byte buffer before a single scanline has been encoded. An ASan build of Pillow does not flag this, because the out-of-bounds stores happen inside the (uninstrumented) system libjpeg-turbo; valgrind does, reporting `Invalid write ... 0 bytes after a block of size 65,569` from `jpeg_write_marker` called at `JpegEncode.c:330` before aborting on the corrupted heap metadata.  ### Code path  The buffer. `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes the encoder buffer from the metadata it is about to emit, allowing one spare byte after the extra block and nothing for the comment:  ```python # src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py:859-862     else:         # The EXIF info needs to be written as one block, + APP1, + one spare byte.         # Ensure that our buffer is big enough. Same with the icc_profile block.         bufsize = max(len(exif) + 5, len(extra) + 1) ```  `ImageFile._save()` then takes `max(MAXBLOCK, bufsize, width*4)` (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:662`, `MAXBLOCK = 65536`), and `_encode()` allocates exactly that: `buf = PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, bufsize)` (`src/encode.c:134`; the real-file path `_encode_to_file()` does `malloc(bufsize)` at `src/encode.c:190`). For the input above `len(extra) == 65516`, so the buffer is 65536 bytes. The `optimize`/`progressive` branch just above (`JpegImagePlugin.py:846-858`) is not immune: its `bufsize` adds `w*h` (or `2*w*h`), but the image dimensions and the ICC length both come from the file, so an exact fit is still constructible there (e.g. with a 19×1 image).  The "+1 spare byte" does not account for what libjpeg itself has already put in the buffer: in state 1 `jpeg_start_compress(&cinfo, TRUE)` (`JpegEncode.c:279`) emits SOI + JFIF APP0, 20 bytes for an RGB source. State 3 then copies the extra block, clamped to the space remaining:  ```c // src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:302-337         case 3:             if (context->extra) {                 unsigned int n = context->extra_size - context->extra_offset;                 if (n > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {                     n = context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer;                 }                 memcpy(context->destination.pub.next_output_byte, context->extra + context->extra_offset, n);                 context->destination.pub.next_output_byte += n;                 context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer -= n;                 context->extra_offset += n;                 if (context->extra_offset >= context->extra_size) {                     state->state++;                 // done -> fall into case 4, even with free_in_buffer == 0                 } else {                     break;                 }             } …          case 4:             if (context->comment) {                 jpeg_write_marker(&context->cinfo, JPEG_COM,                                   (unsigned char *)context->comment, context->comment_size);   // :330 — no space check             }             state->state++;          case 5:             if (1024 > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {   // passes: free_in_buffer is now ~2^64                 break;             }             … jpeg_write_scanlines(…) … ```  Every other emitting state is guarded — state 2 requires `rawExifLen + 5 <= free_in_buffer` (`:287`), state 5 requires 1024 free bytes (`:340`), state 6 requires 100 (`:368`). State 4 has no guard at all. The unguarded `jpeg_write_marker()` call was introduced in `e50ae85ea406` ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0; at 9.3.0 the same input re-saves correctly.  With 20 header bytes plus 65516 extra bytes the copy consumes the buffer to the byte (`free_in_buffer == 0`) and, because the extra block is complete, control falls straight into state 4. One re-wrapped ICC APP2 segment costs 18 bytes of overhead (`JpegImagePlugin.py:788-806`), hence the 65498-byte profile payload. Pillow's destination manager cannot suspend (`empty_output_buffer()` returns FALSE, `JpegEncode.c:45-48`), which is why a *nearly* full buffer is harmless: with 1..N free bytes the comment write decrements `free_in_buffer` to 0 part-way, libjpeg raises `JERR_CANT_SUSPEND`, and the save fails with `OSError: broken data stream`. Only the exact-fit case skips that check, because libjpeg-turbo's marker writer is  ```c /* jcmarker.c */   *(dest->next_output_byte)++ = (JOCTET)val;   if (--dest->free_in_buffer == 0) { if (!(*dest->empty_output_buffer)(cinfo)) ERREXIT(cinfo, JERR_CANT_SUSPEND); } ```  i.e. it writes `buf[65536]` first and then wraps the counter. From there nothing limits the stream: the comment (up to 65533 attacker-chosen bytes) is written verbatim, state 5's 1024-byte check passes against the wrapped counter, and `jpeg_write_scanlines()` appends the full compressed image (≈100 KB for a 256×256 noisy source; proportional to the picture for larger ones). If the process survives that, `ImagingJpegEncode()` returns `next_output_byte - buf` (≈167000) as the byte count and `_encode()` calls `_PyBytes_Resize(&buf, 167199)` on the 65536-byte object, which is where glibc usually notices the smashed neighbouring chunk. Unlike `exif` and `xmp`, there is no length check on the comment in `_save()`. A PNG source works the same way: its `iCCP` chunk becomes `im.info["icc_profile"]` and a `tEXt` chunk keyed `comment` becomes `im.info["comment"]` (and, being zlib-compressed, the file is only ~60 KB); that variant was also confirmed to crash. `thumbnail()` and `convert()` carry `im.info` along, so the usual `open → thumbnail → convert("RGB") → save("JPEG", icc_profile=…)` handler reaches the same state. `xmp=` and `extra=` feed the same `extra` block (33 bytes of overhead for the XMP APP1) and reach the same state. If the application also forwards EXIF, the exact-fit condition becomes `len(extra) + len(exif) + 4 == 65516`, both lengths again taken from the file. The comment length is irrelevant to triggering: a 17-byte `"Created with GIMP"` comment crashes the stock build just as reliably (SIGSEGV in `jpeg_write_scanlines`), it only changes how many of the out-of-bounds bytes are chosen verbatim by the attacker.  ### What lies behind the buffer  The buffer is `PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, 65536)` = `malloc(65569)`, a 0x10030-byte glibc chunk, so `buf[65536]` is the first byte of the next chunk's header. In the same `encode()` call, right after that allocation, `jpeg_start_compress()` `malloc`s libjpeg's PERMANENT pool (chunk 0xa40) and IMAGE pool (chunk 0x3f00); on a groomed or fresh heap these sit directly behind the buffer. The next thing `ImagingJpegEncode()` does after the COM write (`JpegEncode.c:352`; the state-5 room check passes because `free_in_buffer` has wrapped) is call `jpeg_write_scanlines()`, which dispatches through the method tables in that IMAGE pool before any allocator call touches the heap. In the SIGSEGV layout observed on the stock build the fault is at `jpeg_write_scanlines+133: call *0x8(%rax)` with `%rax` pointing just past the end of the buffer at memory now holding comment bytes — an indirect call through a function pointer (`cinfo->main->process_data`) read from bytes the file supplied.  ## Impact  Any service that accepts JPEG uploads and re-encodes them as JPEG while preserving the embedded ICC profile (`icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")` — thumbnailers, CMS and e-commerce image pipelines, Django/Flask upload handlers) can be made to perform a linear heap overwrite starting immediately after a 65536-byte buffer: 4 marker bytes, then up to 65533 bytes taken verbatim from the file's COM segment, then tens to hundreds of kilobytes of compressed image data. No non-default Pillow setting is involved and the file is an otherwise valid 140–210 KB JPEG that decodes normally. The dependable outcome is termination of the worker process by SIGSEGV or a glibc heap-consistency abort (not a Python exception), i.e. denial of service of everything that process serves.  It does not stop at a crash. Both the length and the content of the first 64 KB written out of bounds are attacker-chosen, the victim buffer is an ordinary `malloc` chunk, and what `jpeg_start_compress()` allocates directly behind it — libjpeg's PERMANENT and IMAGE pools, including the method pointers `jpeg_write_scanlines()` calls through immediately afterwards — is predictable. Fixing it reduces those leaks to disclosures rather than footholds.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script. It uses the Pillow already built in `/src` and needs no rebuild. Run it as `./repro`. The last line of output is `BUG` or `OK`.  The script builds a valid 256×256 baseline JPEG from deterministic noise, so the compressed image data comes to about 100 KB. Right after SOI it adds an APP2 `ICC_PROFILE` segment (sequence 1 of 1) with a payload of `65536 - 20 - 18 = 65498` bytes. When Pillow re-encodes the image, libjpeg first writes 20 bytes of SOI and JFIF APP0, and then Pillow copies the re-wrapped ICC segment: 18 bytes of header plus the payload. Together those fill the 65536-byte encoder buffer to the last byte. The constants at the top of the script spell out this arithmetic.  Each file goes through the same application code in a child `python3 -X faulthandler` process:  ```python im = Image.open(BytesIO(data)) im.save(BytesIO(), "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info["icc_profile"]) ```  1. **Control.** The file has the ICC profile but no COM segment. The save returns normally with exit status 0, which shows that the exact-fit ICC profile alone is harmless. 2. **PoC.** This is the same file plus a COM segment of 65533 `C` bytes. `JpegImagePlugin._save()` forwards `im.info["comment"]` automatically. Case 4 of `ImagingJpegEncode()` writes the COM marker into the full buffer, the `free_in_buffer` counter wraps, and the comment and the entire compressed image are written past the end of the heap buffer.  Expected output: the control prints `save returned normally` and `-> exit status 0`. For the PoC, faulthandler prints `Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault` (sometimes a glibc message such as `realloc(): invalid next size` followed by `Aborted`). The Python stack ends in `ImageFile._encode_tile` called from `im.save`, then `-> exit status -11` (or `-6`), and finally `BUG`. The verdict is `BUG` only if the PoC child was killed by a signal. A normal return or a Python exception such as `OSError` gives `OK`.  ## Suggested fix  The attached patch guards state 4 the way state 2 guards the EXIF marker: before calling `jpeg_write_marker()` it requires room for the 4-byte marker header plus the comment plus libjpeg's one-byte slack (`emit_byte` must never bring `free_in_buffer` to 0 with a non-suspending destination), and otherwise returns to the caller for a fresh buffer:  ```diff --- a/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c +++ b/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c @@ -327,6 +327,11 @@          case 4:                if (context->comment) { +                // check for comment len + 'COM' header bytes +                if (context->comment_size + 5 > +                    context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) { +                    break; +                }                  jpeg_write_marker( ```  The encoder then returns with the buffer full, `_encode_tile()` calls it again with an empty buffer, and the comment is emitted there. The C hunk is not sufficient on its own: state 4, like state 2, relies on the Python side guaranteeing that an *empty* buffer is always large enough, and a 65533-byte comment needs 65538 bytes against a 65536-byte `MAXBLOCK` buffer — with only the C guard the encoder returns 0 bytes and no error forever and `_encode_tile()` spins. The patch therefore also changes `JpegImagePlugin._save()` to reserve `len(comment) + 5` in both sizing branches (added to `bufsize` in the `optimize`/`progressive` branch, and as a third term of the `max()` in the plain branch), and normalises the comment to `bytes` first (`str` is UTF-8-encoded, `None` becomes `b""`) so the length is exact for non-ASCII `str` comments; `encode.c` already UTF-8-encodes `str` via `z#`, so the bytes written are unchanged. A side effect visible to users: comments of up to 65533 bytes now save successfully in cases that previously raised `OSError: broken data stream` because the default buffer was too small. The patch adds `test_icc_big_comment` to `Tests/test_file_jpeg.py`, which round-trips a 65533-byte comment with ICC profiles sized around the exact-fit boundary; it crashes (or raises `OSError`) on the unpatched tree and passes with the patch. With the patch applied to a clean tree and rebuilt, the reproducer no longer triggers, and `Tests/test_file_jpeg.py` and `Tests/test_file_mpo.py` pass.  The C guard still depends on the Python sizing to avoid a 0-byte/no-error busy loop, exactly as state 2 already does. A more defensive variant would fail with `IMAGING_CODEC_MEMORY` instead of `break` when the marker does not fit and nothing has been written to the current buffer yet (`next_output_byte == buf`), so that a sizing mistake in any caller can never turn into a busy loop. It would also be consistent with `exif`/`xmp` handling for `_save()` to reject comments longer than `MAX_BYTES_IN_MARKER` (65533) with `ValueError("Comment is too long")` rather than leaving it to libjpeg's `JERR_BAD_LENGTH` → `OSError`.  Independently, the "+ 1 spare byte" / "+ 5" reasoning in `_save()` under-counts by the 18–20 bytes `jpeg_start_compress()` writes before the EXIF/extra blocks; that is what lets attacker-sized metadata land the buffer on an exact boundary in the first place. The attached patch does not change that accounting.  ## The patch  Check free output-buffer space before writing the JPEG COM marker in ImagingJpegEncode, and size the encoder buffer for the comment in JpegImagePlugin._save  Applies to `src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c` at the commit above.  ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py b/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py index b361aef2e..f884883c4 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py @@ -227,6 +227,16 @@ class TestFileJpeg:          im1 = self.roundtrip(hopper(), icc_profile=icc_profile)          assert im1.info.get("icc_profile") == (icc_profile or None)   +    def test_icc_big_comment(self) -> None: +        # The ICC profile may fill the encoder buffer exactly, in which case the +        # comment has to be written to the next buffer +        comment = b"C" * 65533 +        for n in range(ImageFile.MAXBLOCK - 40, ImageFile.MAXBLOCK - 30): +            icc_profile = b"I" * n +            im = self.roundtrip(hopper(), icc_profile=icc_profile, comment=comment) +            assert im.info["icc_profile"] == icc_profile +            assert im.info["comment"] == comment +      def test_large_icc_meta(self, tmp_path: Path) -> None:          # https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/issues/148          # Sometimes the meta data on the icc_profile block is bigger than diff --git a/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py index 4b8d34ca3..1d9f4c2fa 100644 --- a/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py @@ -805,7 +805,9 @@ def _save(im: Image.Image, fp: IO[bytes], filename: str | bytes) -> None:              )              i += 1   - Same with the icc_profile block. -        bufsize = max(len(exif) + 5, len(extra) + 1) +        # Ensure that our buffer is big enough. ### Summary  Every Pillow wheel from 11.1.0 onward bundles a libopenjp2 containing a heap-buffer-overflow **write** that is fixed upstream on master but has never appeared in an OpenJPEG release. See https://osv.dev/vulnerability/OSV-2025-219  Because the wheel bundles its own copy, a patched host OS does not help. It is reachable from `Image.open(fp); im.load()` with default settings.  I am reporting it here rather than only upstream because Pillow is where the vulnerable binary actually reaches users.  Note the inversion that makes this easy to miss: **OpenJPEG 2.5.2 and earlier are safe.** The bug was introduced in `954c6e3c` (2024-06-25), so keeping the dependency current is what creates the exposure.  ### Details  ## Affected wheels  From `.github/dependencies.json` (`openjpeg`) at each tag:  | Pillow | bundled OpenJPEG | status | |---|---|---| | 10.4.0 | 2.5.2 | safe | | 11.0.0 | 2.5.2 | safe | | **11.1.0, 11.2.1, 11.3.0** | **2.5.3** | **affected** | | **12.0.0 … 12.3.0** | **2.5.4** | **affected** |  Confirmed on an installed wheel: `PIL.features.version_codec('jpg_2000')` → `2.5.4`, bundled file `pillow.libs/libopenjp2-*.so.2.5.4`. `main` still pins `2.5.4` as of 2026-10-06.  ## The defect  `src/lib/openjp2/j2k.c`, in `opj_j2k_read_sod`:  ```c OPJ_UINT32 l_current_tile_part =     l_cstr_index->tile_index[p_j2k->m_current_tile_number].current_tpsno; l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_header = l_current_pos; l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_pos   =     l_current_pos + p_j2k->m_specific_param.m_decoder.m_sot_length + 2; ```  `tp_index` is neither null-checked nor bounds-checked, and `l_current_tile_part` comes directly from the one-byte `TPsot` field of the SOT marker.  The correct guard already exists a few lines later in `opj_j2k_add_tlmarker` (j2k.c:8459), writing the **same array at the same index** behind `if (tp_index && l_current_tile_part < nb_tps)`. One writer checked, its sibling not.  Reached by giving the codestream a *valid* TLM marker — so `tp_index` is allocated once by `opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm`, sized to the TLM entry count, and `opj_j2k_read_sot` then skips all resizing — while setting `TNsot = 0` in every SOT, which keeps the TLM "valid" and lets `TPsot` walk past the allocation.  ## Patch status  Fixed upstream in `91d08b11` ("Fix heap buffer overlfow in opj_j2k_read_sod", 2026-02-10).  The newest OpenJPEG tag is **v2.5.4 (2025-09-20)**, and `compare/v2.5.4...91d08b11` reports *ahead 6, behind 0* — the fix is **in no release, 8 months on**.  ## Suggested remediation  1. Carry `91d08b11` as a patch in the wheel build until an OpenJPEG release includes it — three lines, identical to a guard already present in the same file. 2. Consider asking OpenJPEG to cut a release; they have had an unreleased memory-corruption fix on master since February 2026, and every distro is shipping the vulnerable code. 3. Your security handbook already tells applications to block EPS at the application layer. A similarly explicit note that `Image.open()` ignores filename/Content-Type and will reach any compiled-in codec unless `formats=` is passed would help downstream apps a lot.  ## Not a Pillow bug, but relevant: the extension allowlist most apps rely on does not apply  `Image.open()` sniffs magic bytes, so a JPEG 2000 codestream in a file named `avatar.png` declared `Content-Type: image/png` reaches the JP2 decoder anyway.  I verified this against a production service documenting PNG/JPEG-only uploads: it accepted and fully decoded a JP2 through exactly that path, with 16 formats reachable from one upload endpoint against 43 registered openers. That service has since fixed it by passing `formats=` and validating on the detected format rather than the client's `Content-Type`.  That is the reason a decoder-level issue like this one has much wider reach than downstream maintainers tend to assume.  ### Proof of concept  ASan build of OpenJPEG 2.5.4 interposed under a **stock Pillow 12.3.0**, running `Image.open(p); im.load()`:  ``` ==766332==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow WRITE of size 8     #0 opj_j2k_read_sod          j2k.c:5086     #1 opj_j2k_read_tile_header  j2k.c:9912     #2 opj_read_tile_header      openjpeg.c:575     #3 j2k_decode_entry          src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:793     #4 ImagingJpeg2KDecode       src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:949     #5 _decode                   src/decode.c:132 located 8 bytes to the right of a 24-byte region allocated by     opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm j2k.c:8939 ```  Frames 3–5 are Pillow's own decoder, not a synthetic harness. No non-default decoder options are involved; strict mode is on, which is Pillow's behaviour since Pillow never calls `opj_decoder_set_strict_mode`. A benign twin image runs the same path cleanly and returns a valid image, so this is the payload and not a parse failure.  I have deliberately **not** attached the PoC file to this initial report. I'm happy to attach the PoC, the builder script and the RIP-control harness here on request, or hold everything until a fix is ready.  No disclosure deadline from me; I will not publish anything while this is being worked on.  ### Impact  Any application that calls `Image.open()` / `im.load()` on an image it did not produce — the overwhelmingly common case for upload handlers, thumbnailers and preview pipelines — can be made to perform an out-of-bounds heap write by supplying one crafted file.  **Floor, already certain.** On a stock non-sanitised wheel the overflow performs 245 writes walking to +5856 bytes past a 24-byte allocation, and glibc's own heap-metadata checker aborts the process (`corrupted size vs. prev_size`, `corrupted double-linked list`, SIGABRT). One file reliably kills a long-lived worker.  **Ceiling, demonstrated as a primitive but not as a finished exploit.** With same-size-class objects alive on both sides — an ordinary busy heap — the walk crosses `opj_event_mgr_t`, which holds three `opj_msg_callback` function pointers, and `opj_event_msg` then calls one (event.c:136):  ``` rip  0x4000    <- value chosen by the attacker's file layout rsi  0x3ff2    <- m_error_data, written by the same walk ```  Shifting the codestream with a COM marker moves `rip` with it (`0x16ce` → `0x4000`), so the instruction pointer is attacker-**chosen** rather than incidentally invalid. A benign control image leaves the same groomed heap untouched.  To be explicit about what I did not do: I have **not** built a working exploit. That additionally needs remote heap grooming and an ASLR defeat, and I attempted neither. I am reporting a controlled control-flow primitive, not a finished chain. The CVSS AC:H reflects that.

When extracting a tar archive pip may not check symbolic links point into the extraction directory if the tarfile module doesn't implement PEP 706. Note that upgrading pip to a "fixed" version for this vulnerability doesn't fix all known vulnerabilities that are remediated by using a Python version that implements PEP 706. Note that this is a vulnerability in pip's fallback implementation of tar extraction for Python versions that don't implement PEP 706 and therefore are not secure to all vulnerabilities in the Python 'tarfile' module. If you're using a Python version that implements PEP 706 then pip doesn't use the "vulnerable" fallback code. Mitigations include upgrading to a version of pip that includes the fix, upgrading to a Python version that implements PEP 706 (Python >=3.9.17, >=3.10.12, >=3.11.4, or >=3.12), applying the linked patch, or inspecting source distributions (sdists) before installation as is already a best-practice.

When pip is installing and extracting a maliciously crafted wheel archive, files may be extracted outside the installation directory. The path traversal is limited to prefixes of the installation directory, thus isn't able to inject or overwrite executable files in typical situations.

pip handles concatenated tar and ZIP files as ZIP files regardless of filename or whether a file is both a tar and ZIP file. This behavior could result in confusing installation behavior, such as installing "incorrect" files according to the filename of the archive. New behavior only proceeds with installation if the file identifies uniquely as a ZIP or tar archive, not as both.

These module imports were intentionally deferred to increase startup time of the pip CLI. The patch changes self-update functionality to run before wheels are installed to prevent newly-installed modules from being imported shortly after the installation of a wheel package. Users should still review package contents prior to installation.

### Impact The BER/CER/DER decoders process OBJECT IDENTIFIER and RELATIVE-OID values in quadratic time relative to the number of arcs. A small crafted payload (tens of kilobytes) containing an OID with many arcs consumes seconds of CPU per decode() call, allowing denial of service in any application that decodes untrusted ASN.1 data (certificates, LDAP, SNMP, Kerberos, etc.). The corresponding encoders have the same quadratic behavior, reachable when an application re-encodes previously decoded attacker-supplied values.  The arc-size limit introduced for CVE-2026-23490 bounds the byte length of an individual arc but not the number of arcs, so it does not mitigate this issue.  ### Affected components ObjectIdentifierPayloadDecoder and RelativeOIDPayloadDecoder in pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py; ObjectIdentifierEncoder and RelativeOIDEncoder in pyasn1/codec/ber/encoder.py. The CER and DER codecs inherit these and are equally affected.  ### Patches Fixed in pyasn1 0.6.4: arc accumulation in both decoders and encoders now runs in linear time.  ### Workarounds Limit the size of untrusted ASN.1 input before decoding.

### Impact The univ.Real type converted its (mantissa, base, exponent) value to a Python float using exact big-integer exponentiation. A BER/CER/DER-encoded REAL value only a few bytes long can carry a very large exponent, causing this computation to attempt to materialize an astronomically large integer.  Any operation that triggers float conversion on such a decoded value — prettyPrint(), str(), comparison, arithmetic, or an explicit float() call — consumes excessive CPU and memory, hanging the process. Applications that decode untrusted ASN.1 data and then print, log, or compare the decoded objects are vulnerable to denial of service. Decoding alone does not trigger the issue.  ### Affected components - pyasn1.type.univ.Real — float conversion (__float__() and everything built on it: prettyPrint(), str(), comparisons, arithmetic, int()) - Reachable through the pyasn1.codec.ber, cer, and der decoders, which produce Real objects from untrusted input; also via directly constructed Real values  The encoders and the native codec are not affected. Applications that never handle ASN.1 REAL values are not affected.  ### Patches Fixed in pyasn1 0.6.4. Binary (base-2) values are now converted with math.ldexp(), and decimal (base-10) values with exponents beyond float range raise OverflowError without constructing huge intermediate integers. Existing behavior is preserved: out-of-range values raise OverflowError and prettyPrint() renders them as <overflow>.  ### Workarounds Avoid converting, printing, or comparing decoded Real objects from untrusted sources; inspect the raw (mantissa, base, exponent) tuple instead.
